pieces.label: What an ISO is, and how to look around a machine — scenario
pieces.text: Somebody has handed you a machine and asked a simple question: what is on it? You could poke at it with a mouse, but the honest way to answer — the way every system administrator answers, and the way every person who has built an ISO answers — is to open a terminal and look. This lab is that, once, slowly: you open a terminal, you find out where you are standing, you look at what is here, and you read a file. Later labs build an ISO image on top of exactly these skills, so nothing here is a warm-up for its own sake.

pieces.label: What an ISO is, and how to look around a machine — the lesson
pieces.text: A terminal is a window into a machine. You type a line of text, press Enter, and the machine answers. There is no mouse involved, and nothing is hidden: every word you type does something you can see. A command is one of those lines. It starts with the name of a program, like ls or cat, followed by the words that say what to work on. A command is not a sentence and it needs no punctuation — just the program name, a space, and what you want it to act on. A file path is the name of a file written as a chain of folders separated by slashes. A path that starts with a slash is absolute: it means the same place on the machine no matter where you are standing, so /home/learner always means that one folder. A path without a leading slash is relative: it means "this, starting from the folder you are standing in", so notes means the notes folder inside wherever you happen to be. An ISO image is a single file that contains an entire filesystem — a whole operating system, its programs and its settings, packed into one file you can copy around and write to a USB stick, where it becomes a computer that boots without touching the computer's own drive. You would want to build one when you want a system that exists in a form you control: the exact programs, nothing extra, ready to boot on a machine you have never seen. And because an ISO image is just a file, you can keep it in a version history, put it on a server, and hand it to somebody else. A package is one piece of software, packaged up so it can be installed and removed as one unit, and a package manager is the program that does that installing and removing. You do not need to know anything about packages yet. You do need to know that this machine has a file system, folders, and files inside them, because that is what an ISO image is a picture of.

pieces.label: What an ISO is, and how to look around a machine — The machine in front of you
pieces.text:
The terminal below is a practice machine. It is a small, honest copy of a Linux machine: it has folders, it has files with text in them, and commands change it for real. Nothing you do in here can break anything on your own computer.

You start in /home/learner. That is your home folder — the folder that belongs to you, in the same way that your own home folder belongs to you. There are two things in it: a README.txt file, and a folder called notes.

If you get lost, or you break something, press "Reset lab". It puts the machine back exactly as it started, and it is always allowed.

pieces.label: What an ISO is, and how to look around a machine — How a command answers you
pieces.text:
Every command answers in the same shape. First comes output: the normal answer to what you asked. Sometimes there is an error as well, printed underneath. An error is not a punishment and it is not a wrong answer from you — it is the machine telling you that it could not do what you asked, and why.

If you type something the machine does not recognise at all, it says "command not found". That nearly always means one of two things: a typo, or a program that is not installed on this machine.

Errors are part of the lesson, not a detour from it. In later labs the error messages are the most informative thing on the screen.

pieces.label: What an ISO is, and how to look around a machine — Where an ISO comes from
pieces.text:
An ISO image does not appear on its own. You describe it first, in a plain text file called a profile: what the image is called, what it contains, and which packages go into it. You then hand that description to a tool called archiso, and archiso builds the image from it.

So the path you are on in this lab — a folder of text files that describe something — is the same shape as the thing you will build later. That is why this lab is worth doing slowly.

pieces.label: What an ISO is, and how to look around a machine — task: Find out where you are standing. The command that prints this is called pwd. Then save the answer in a file called where-i-am.txt in your home folder.
pieces.text:
Find out where you are standing. The command that prints this is called pwd. Then save the answer in a file called where-i-am.txt in your home folder.

Try `pwd` on its own first and read what it prints. Then try `pwd > where-i-am.txt` and see what happens.

Two steps: `pwd` to see the path, then `pwd > where-i-am.txt` to save that same answer into a file called where-i-am.txt.

Every other path on this machine is measured from wherever you are standing, so knowing where that is makes every path you use afterwards mean what you think it means. This is the first thing anyone does when they open a terminal on a machine they have never seen.

pieces.label: What an ISO is, and how to look around a machine — task: Now look at what is in this folder. The command that lists what is here is called ls. One of the names it prints is a folder called notes — move into it with cd.
pieces.text:
Now look at what is in this folder. The command that lists what is here is called ls. One of the names it prints is a folder called notes — move into it with cd.

`ls` lists the names of the files and folders in the folder you are standing in. `cd` moves you into one of them.

Run `ls` first, look for `notes`, then `cd notes`.

Listing tells you what you could open. Changing folder tells you what you will open by default. A path like `notes` only means something because you know where you are standing — that is why the first task came before this one.

pieces.label: What an ISO is, and how to look around a machine — task: Open iso-notes.txt in this folder and find the line that says what an ISO image is. Copy that line into a new file called answer.txt that lives in your home folder: /home/learner/answer.txt.
pieces.text:
Open iso-notes.txt in this folder and find the line that says what an ISO image is. Copy that line into a new file called answer.txt that lives in your home folder: /home/learner/answer.txt.

`cat iso-notes.txt` shows you the whole file. `grep` picks out only the lines you ask for. And because you are standing in the notes folder, the answer file needs its full path — /home/learner/answer.txt — to land in your home folder.

`grep "ISO image is one file" iso-notes.txt > /home/learner/answer.txt` writes just that one line into the file.

Reading is the skill; the file is only proof that you did it. Copying a line out of one file and into another is the most common thing anyone ever does in a shell, and it is exactly how a profile gets built out of pieces.

pieces.label: What an ISO is, and how to look around a machine — task: Make a folder for your own notes, called my-notes, in your home folder — the same place where where-i-am.txt is. You are standing in the notes folder, so this is a good moment to use a full path.
pieces.text:
Make a folder for your own notes, called my-notes, in your home folder — the same place where where-i-am.txt is. You are standing in the notes folder, so this is a good moment to use a full path.

A path that starts with a slash is absolute — the same folder wherever you stand. A path without one is relative — "inside wherever you are now", which right now is the notes folder.

`mkdir /home/learner/my-notes`

When you build an ISO, the shape of your folders is the shape of the image. Knowing which of the two kinds of path you just used is the difference between a folder in the right place and a folder you cannot find later.

pieces.label: What an ISO is, and how to look around a machine — task: Put something in your new folder: a file called first-note.txt inside my-notes. Copy the notes file into it to get started, then read your copy back with cat so you know it really arrived.
pieces.text:
Put something in your new folder: a file called first-note.txt inside my-notes. Copy the notes file into it to get started, then read your copy back with cat so you know it really arrived.

`cp` copies one file to another name and leaves the original alone. `cat` prints a file back to you. Use the full paths for both, because the folder you are standing in is not the folder you are writing to.

`cp /home/learner/notes/iso-notes.txt /home/learner/my-notes/first-note.txt`, then `cat /home/learner/my-notes/first-note.txt`.

This is the whole loop of the lab: look, read, copy, read back. Reading a file back is how you confirm it is really there instead of trusting that it is. Later in the academy, the file you write will be a profile, and the profile is what becomes the ISO.

pieces.label: What an ISO is, and how to look around a machine — the point
pieces.text: You opened a terminal on a machine you had never seen and you found out what was on it: where you were, what was in the folder, what the notes said, and what you could put somewhere new. Those five moves — look, list, read, make, write — are the whole of working in a shell. An ISO image is built out of exactly them.

pieces.label: pacman: searching, installing, removing — scenario
pieces.text: Your profile says which packages belong on the image. Every one of those names is a package that pacman knows about, and pacman is what turns the names into files on a filesystem. Before you write a single line of a profile, you need to know what pacman actually does with that list: how to find a package, how to look at one before you trust it, how to install it, how to take it away again, and what a full update really means. This lab is a practice machine with pacman on it, and it is deliberately built so that some of the things you try will fail — because the errors are where the real understanding comes from.

pieces.label: pacman: searching, installing, removing — the lesson
pieces.text: A package is one piece of software, packaged up so that it can be installed and removed as a single unit: a text editor, a web browser, a kernel. A package manager is the program that works with those packages — it downloads them, checks what they need, installs them, removes them, and keeps a list of what is installed. On Arch Linux the package manager is pacman, and the places it downloads from are called repositories. Here is why an ISO builder cares about any of this: the package list in a profile is a pacman list. When the image is built, that list is handed to pacman inside a brand new, empty filesystem, and pacman installs every name in it. So a name in your profile is not a label — it is an instruction, and pacman will stop the whole build on a name it does not recognise. Nobody should edit one of those lists without knowing what pacman does with it. The commands in this lab are the ones you will use every single time: pacman -Ss searches the repositories for a name, pacman -Qi shows you everything pacman knows about one package, pacman -S installs one, pacman -R removes one, pacman -Q lists what is installed, and pacman -Syu is a full update — the -Sy part refreshes pacman's copy of the repository lists and the -u part upgrades everything that is installed. A full update is a step of its own, done on purpose, not bundled into every install.

pieces.label: pacman: searching, installing, removing — The commands, and what each one is for
pieces.text:
pacman -Ss <word> — search the repositories. It prints the exact package name, its version, and one line describing it. You use this when you know roughly what you want but not what it is called.

pacman -Qi <name> — show information about one package: name, version, description, which repository it comes from, how big it is, and what it depends on. It works before the package is installed.

pacman -S <name> — install. pacman -R <name> — remove. pacman -Q — list every installed package, one name per line. pacman -Q <name> — ask about that one package.

pacman -Syu — the full update. -Sy refreshes the repository lists, -u upgrades the installed packages.

pieces.label: pacman: searching, installing, removing — Reading a pacman error
pieces.text:
Pacman refuses things. It will not install a package whose name it does not know, because it will not guess: a name that is one character off is not "nearly right", it is a different thing that does not exist.

When that happens, pacman says so plainly: "error: package 'something' was not found". The name in the message is the name pacman could not find. Usually the name you wanted is one search away.

The same message comes back when you ask about a package that is not installed. That failure is not a fault. It is how pacman says "no, and here is what I do know".

The removal in this lab is done on the base package that came with the machine, because that is the one package already here to take off. On a real system you would remove something you had installed yourself.

pieces.label: pacman: searching, installing, removing — What an update really is
pieces.text:
Pacman keeps a local copy of the lists of packages the repositories offer. Those copies go stale, and when they are stale pacman is working from yesterday's idea of what exists.

A full update fixes that in two moves: -Sy refreshes the copies, -u upgrades everything already installed against the fresh copies. Do it as its own step, deliberately, so you know the database was current before you chose what to install. On a real machine `pacman -Syu` on its own updates everything; on this practice machine an update needs a package name to act on.

pieces.label: pacman: searching, installing, removing — task: Look before you install. Search the repositories for a text editor with `pacman -Ss nano` — it prints the package name, its version, and one line describing it — and then install it with `pacman -S nano`.
pieces.text:
Look before you install. Search the repositories for a text editor with `pacman -Ss nano` — it prints the package name, its version, and one line describing it — and then install it with `pacman -S nano`.

The search flag is a capital S with a small s: -Ss. The install flag is a capital S on its own: -S. The word you search for goes after the flag.

`pacman -Ss nano` to look, then `pacman -S nano` to install.

Searching first tells you the exact name and what the package claims to be. Pacman will not guess at a name for you, so one wrong character in a profile is a build that stops halfway. Five seconds of searching now is the difference later.

pieces.label: pacman: searching, installing, removing — task: Now do it the careful way, with a second package. Look at curl before you install it: `pacman -Qi curl` shows its version, its description, which repository it comes from and how big it is. Read it, then install it.
pieces.text:
Now do it the careful way, with a second package. Look at curl before you install it: `pacman -Qi curl` shows its version, its description, which repository it comes from and how big it is. Read it, then install it.

A capital Q with a small i means "give me information about this package". It works on a package that is not installed yet, which is exactly when you want it.

`pacman -Qi curl` to read about it, then `pacman -S curl` to install it.

A package name in a profile is a promise about what will be on the image. Reading the description before you install is how you find out whether you are promising the right thing — and whether the thing is really in the official repositories.

pieces.label: pacman: searching, installing, removing — task: Now see the whole picture. `pacman -Q` lists every installed package, one name per line. Look at that list, then add one more package to it: `pacman -S vim`.
pieces.text:
Now see the whole picture. `pacman -Q` lists every installed package, one name per line. Look at that list, then add one more package to it: `pacman -S vim`.

A capital Q with nothing after it lists everything. A capital S with a package name after it installs that package.

`pacman -Q` to read the list, then `pacman -S vim`.

That list is the profile. When an ISO is built, pacman is handed exactly this list and installs each name into a brand new filesystem. On a real machine you would save it into a file and hand that file to the profile — which is why it is worth knowing how to read it.

pieces.label: pacman: searching, installing, removing — task: Now take something back off. This machine came with a small set already installed: base, bash and pacman. Remove the base package with `pacman -R base`, then ask pacman about it again with `pacman -Q base`. This time it should fail, and that failure is the confirmation that it is gone.
pieces.text:
Now take something back off. This machine came with a small set already installed: base, bash and pacman. Remove the base package with `pacman -R base`, then ask pacman about it again with `pacman -Q base`. This time it should fail, and that failure is the confirmation that it is gone.

Removal is a capital R. The capital Q afterwards is the same command that lists installed packages — with a name after it, it asks about that one package only.

`pacman -R base`, then `pacman -Q base`, and read what it says.

An image is only as good as the list that built it, and knowing how to take things off is how you keep a profile honest. Learning that a package which is gone reports an error rather than silence is how you notice, before a build, that a name in your list is not real. (base is a metapackage — really a list of other packages — so removing it does not take the rest of the system with it.)

pieces.label: pacman: searching, installing, removing — task: Now the update. A full update is `pacman -Syu`: the -Sy part refreshes pacman's copy of the repository lists, and the -u part upgrades everything that is installed. It is a step of its own, not something you bundle into every install. On this machine an update needs a package to act on, so run a full update that brings the longterm kernel in: `pacman -Syu linux-lts`.
pieces.text:
Now the update. A full update is `pacman -Syu`: the -Sy part refreshes pacman's copy of the repository lists, and the -u part upgrades everything that is installed. It is a step of its own, not something you bundle into every install. On this machine an update needs a package to act on, so run a full update that brings the longterm kernel in: `pacman -Syu linux-lts`.

The three letters go together: -Syu. On a real machine `pacman -Syu` on its own updates everything that is installed. Here you name a package so there is something for it to do.

`pacman -Syu linux-lts`

Updating refreshes what pacman believes is available, and doing it deliberately, as its own step, is what keeps a build reproducible: you know the repository lists were current before you chose the versions. It is also why a profile pins what it wants instead of trusting whatever is newest on the day.

pieces.label: pacman: searching, installing, removing — task: Now meet an error on purpose. Try to install a package that does not exist: type `pacman -S devtool` — the real name has an s on the end. Read what pacman says. It refuses; it will not guess a name for you. Then search for the real one with `pacman -Ss devtools` and install it.
pieces.text:
Now meet an error on purpose. Try to install a package that does not exist: type `pacman -S devtool` — the real name has an s on the end. Read what pacman says. It refuses; it will not guess a name for you. Then search for the real one with `pacman -Ss devtools` and install it.

Read the error carefully: it names the package it could not find. That name is usually one search away from the one you wanted.

`pacman -Ss devtools` to see the real name and version, then `pacman -S devtools`.

This is the failure you will meet in a real build, and the error message is written for exactly this moment. Read it and it tells you the name pacman wanted, which is almost always the name you nearly typed.

pieces.label: pacman: searching, installing, removing — the point
pieces.text: You now know what pacman does with a list of names: it searches for them, it will tell you what each one actually is, it installs them, it removes them, it refuses names it does not recognise, and it updates itself on its own schedule. That list is your profile. From here on, every name you put in it is an instruction to pacman, not a label.

pieces.label: git: the history of your ISO profile — scenario
pieces.text: Your ISO flavour is not a folder on a desktop. It is a repository — a folder whose every change is recorded, with a name and a reason attached — and the build pipeline builds a commit, not a folder. That one fact changes how you work. You can change anything you like, but until the change is committed, nothing builds it and nothing ships it. This lab is that loop once around: a repository, an identity, a staged file, a commit, a branch, and one change you deliberately leave out.

pieces.label: git: the history of your ISO profile — the lesson
pieces.text: A repository — people shorten it to a repo — is a directory that git watches. Alongside your files, git keeps a hidden folder called .git that holds the whole history: every version of every file, and who changed it and when. A commit is one entry in that history. It is a complete snapshot of your files at a moment in time, with a message saying what changed and why, and the name and email of the person who made it. Two more git words you will need today, and they are the ones people mix up: the working tree is your files as they are on disk right now, with your unsaved-to-history edits in them; staged means you have marked a file with git add as "this one belongs in my next commit"; committed means a snapshot that already exists in the history. Here is why any of this matters to an ISO builder: your profile — the recipe that becomes an image — is a repository, and the pipeline builds a commit. It does not build "whatever happens to be on the disk". So if you edit the profile and do not commit it, your edit is invisible to the build: the image will be built from the last commit, and your change will not be in it. That is not a flaw in the pipeline, it is the point of one. Builds are supposed to be reproducible, and the only thing about a set of files that is reproducible is a commit with a name on it. Git has a few other words worth knowing even though this lab does not use them: clone means copying somebody else's repository onto your machine, and push means sending your commits to a server so other people can have them. What follows is the local half of that: init, add, commit, log, branch, status.

pieces.label: git: the history of your ISO profile — The files in this folder
pieces.text:
There are two of them. profiledef.sh is the start of an ISO profile: it is a plain text file that says what the image is called and which packages belong on it. README.txt is a note about the folder.

Both of them are yours to change. Git is not going to stop you — that is the whole point of git. It just records what you did.

pieces.label: git: the history of your ISO profile — The commands, and what each one is for
pieces.text:
git init — turn this folder into a repository. It adds the hidden .git folder and changes nothing else.

git config user.name "..." and git config user.email "..." — tell git who you are. Git records an author on every commit and will not commit without one.

git add <file> — stage a file: mark it as part of the next commit. git add . stages everything in the folder you are standing in.

git commit -m "..." — record everything that is staged, with a message. The -m flag means "message", and the message goes in quotes right after it.

git log — read the history, newest commit first. git status — ask what is staged and what is not. git branch <name> — make a branch, and in this terminal, move onto it.

pieces.label: git: the history of your ISO profile — Why a message matters
pieces.text:
A commit message is not a formality. It is the one sentence that tells whoever reads the history next — including you in six months, and including the pipeline log — what changed and why.

Say what you did and, when it is not obvious, why. "add the profile stub" is fine. "fix" is not.

pieces.label: git: the history of your ISO profile — task: Turn this folder into a repository: `git init`. That creates a hidden .git folder here, and from now on git keeps track of what you change.
pieces.text:
Turn this folder into a repository: `git init`. That creates a hidden .git folder here, and from now on git keeps track of what you change.

The command is two words: `git init`.

`git init`

Everything else in this lab happens inside a repository. Git will refuse to add, commit, or even tell you the status of a folder that is not one, because there is nowhere for it to put the answer.

pieces.label: git: the history of your ISO profile — task: Git stamps every commit with an author, and it needs to know who that is before it will record one. Set your name and your email: `git config user.name "Your Name"` and `git config user.email "you@example.com"`.
pieces.text:
Git stamps every commit with an author, and it needs to know who that is before it will record one. Set your name and your email: `git config user.name "Your Name"` and `git config user.email "you@example.com"`.

Two settings, two commands. The names of the settings are user.name and user.email, and the value goes in quotes after each one.

`git config user.name "Your Name"` and `git config user.email "you@example.com"`

The author line is what turns a pile of changes into a history a person can read. It is also how you know which commit — and therefore which ISO — came out of whose work, when a build turns up an image nobody expected.

pieces.label: git: the history of your ISO profile — task: Look at the two files here: profiledef.sh is the start of an ISO profile, and README.txt is a note. Stage profiledef.sh with `git add`. Staging means "this file belongs in my next commit" — it is not a commit yet.
pieces.text:
Look at the two files here: profiledef.sh is the start of an ISO profile, and README.txt is a note. Stage profiledef.sh with `git add`. Staging means "this file belongs in my next commit" — it is not a commit yet.

Staging is `git add` followed by the file name. `git status` will then tell you what is waiting to be committed.

`git add profiledef.sh`

Staging is where you choose what a commit means. It is the difference between "I edited a file" and "this is the change I am recording", and it is where a careless build gets its wrong contents.

pieces.label: git: the history of your ISO profile — task: Now record it: `git commit -m "your message here"`. The message is a note to whoever reads the history next, so say what changed and why. Then run `git log` to see your commit sitting in the history.
pieces.text:
Now record it: `git commit -m "your message here"`. The message is a note to whoever reads the history next, so say what changed and why. Then run `git log` to see your commit sitting in the history.

The -m flag means "message", and the message goes in quotes right after it. If git says there is nothing to commit, nothing is staged — `git add` the file again.

`git add profiledef.sh`, then `git commit -m "add the profile stub"`, then `git log`.

A commit is the unit the build pipeline takes. It has to say what it contains, because the pipeline will be pointed at it by name, and because the next person to change the profile needs to know what they are building on.

pieces.label: git: the history of your ISO profile — task: You are about to try something, and you want it separate from the main line of work. Make a branch called feature/my-flavour and move onto it — in this terminal, `git branch feature/my-flavour` does both. Then run `git log` again: your history follows you onto the branch.
pieces.text:
You are about to try something, and you want it separate from the main line of work. Make a branch called feature/my-flavour and move onto it — in this terminal, `git branch feature/my-flavour` does both. Then run `git log` again: your history follows you onto the branch.

A branch is a parallel line of work. `git branch` on its own lists the branches; `git branch <name>` makes one, and here it moves you onto it as well.

`git branch feature/my-flavour`, then `git status` to see where you are.

A branch is how you try something without breaking what already works. It matters for the pipeline too: many pipelines build the main branch, so work on a branch is work that is not shipped until somebody merges it on purpose.

pieces.label: git: the history of your ISO profile — task: Now the bit that catches people out. Change one of the two files here — the iso_name line in profiledef.sh is the obvious one; change it to the name of your own ISO — and save it, but do not stage it and do not commit it. Then run `git status` and read what it says about the file.
pieces.text:
Now the bit that catches people out. Change one of the two files here — the iso_name line in profiledef.sh is the obvious one; change it to the name of your own ISO — and save it, but do not stage it and do not commit it. Then run `git status` and read what it says about the file.

`sed -i` edits a file in place, without staging it. Then `cat profiledef.sh` to see your change, and `git status` to see what git makes of it.

Any change will do — change the iso_name line to whatever you want to call your ISO image, and leave it unstaged.

This is the whole reason the lab exists. The build pipeline builds a commit, so a change that is not committed is not in the commit, and therefore not in the ISO. On a real machine `git status` lists that file under "Changes not staged for commit"; this practice terminal only lists what is staged, so what you are looking for is that your file is not among them.

pieces.label: git: the history of your ISO profile — the point
pieces.text: You have a repository with a name and an email attached, a commit with a message that says what it contains, a branch to work on, and a change on your disk that is deliberately not in the history yet. That last one is the point of the whole thing: the pipeline builds a commit, so a change that is not committed is a change that never gets built.

pieces.label: Building a package the proper way — scenario
pieces.text: You want to hand someone a package: a built, installable file for a tiny program called hello, so they can put it on their machine with one command. A package is not a folder of scripts somebody has to run by hand. To make one you need two things — a recipe that says what the program is and how to build it, and a build that produces the same result on your machine and on theirs. This lab is those two things.

pieces.label: Building a package the proper way — the lesson
pieces.text: A package recipe is a shell script called PKGBUILD. It is the same format everywhere: in the official repositories, in the AUR, and in whatever you write yourself. It says what the package is called, which version it is, where the source comes from, and what goes inside the finished package. Nothing about it is magic — pacman, makepkg and the AUR all read the same plain text.

pieces.label: Building a package the proper way — What a PKGBUILD is
pieces.text:
A PKGBUILD is a shell script. Not a configuration format, not a special kind of file — a script. makepkg sources it, so every line in it is run by the shell, and the variables it sets are the recipe: pkgname, pkgver, pkgdesc, arch, depends, and so on.

At the bottom there are usually four functions. prepare() unpacks and patches the source, build() compiles it, check() runs its tests, and package() lays the finished files into the package. That last one is the important one: package() puts files under $pkgdir, and $pkgdir is the directory that becomes / when the package is installed. A recipe never writes to your live system. Ever.

pieces.label: Building a package the proper way — Why a clean chroot
pieces.text:
A clean chroot build is a build that happens inside an empty container holding nothing but the build dependencies. That container is a chroot, and the point of it is that nothing of yours leaks in.

If you build on your own machine, the build inherits every library, header, compiler flag and stray patch you happen to have installed. The result is not a package. It is a snapshot of your desk: it works on a machine shaped like yours, and it breaks on anyone else’s. That is why Arch builds everything in a clean chroot, and why the built file contains only what package() put into $pkgdir.

pieces.label: Building a package the proper way — makepkg and pkgctl
pieces.text:
devtools is the toolkit that does this properly. makepkg reads the PKGBUILD in the directory you are standing in, checks that every dependency in depends is installed, fetches and verifies the sources, runs the four functions, and collects the result into a file named name-version-arch.pkg.tar.zst.

pkgctl is the current front door to devtools. `pkgctl build` is the one-command version of the clean chroot build — the same work, with the modern door in front of it. It is how Arch packaging is actually driven now, and it is the command you should reach for.

pieces.label: Building a package the proper way — task: Give this package a directory of its own. Make a directory called hello in your home and step into it — makepkg only ever reads the PKGBUILD in the directory you are standing in.
pieces.text:
Give this package a directory of its own. Make a directory called hello in your home and step into it — makepkg only ever reads the PKGBUILD in the directory you are standing in.

Check where you are with `pwd`. The build happens wherever the recipe is, so the recipe needs a directory of its own.

Two commands: `mkdir hello`, then `cd hello`.

makepkg builds whatever PKGBUILD sits in the current directory and nowhere else. One package per directory keeps builds from stepping on each other, and it is the same habit that makes a clean chroot build reproducible.

pieces.label: Building a package the proper way — task: Write a PKGBUILD for a tiny program called hello. It prints a greeting it fetches over the network, so it needs curl at run time. The recipe needs at least five things: pkgname (hello), pkgver, pkgdesc (one short line saying what it is), arch (any — it runs anywhere), and depends (curl).

Write a PKGBUILD for a tiny program called hello. It prints a greeting it fetches over the network, so it needs curl at run time. The recipe needs at least five things: pkgname (hello), pkgver, pkgdesc (one short line saying what it is), arch (any — it runs anywhere), and depends (curl).

A PKGBUILD is a shell script of key=value lines. The tidiest way to write one in a single command is printf with a redirect: `printf 'pkgname=hello\npkgver=1.0.0\n' > PKGBUILD`.

Something close to this: pkgname=hello, pkgver=1.0.0, pkgdesc="Fetches and prints a greeting", arch=(any), depends=(curl).

These five lines are the whole contract between you and pacman. The name and version become the file name. The description is what people read when they search. The architecture says who can install it. And depends is the promise that the package will actually run once it is on a machine.

pieces.label: Building a package the proper way — task: Now run makepkg and read what it says. It will refuse to build and name a dependency you do not have. Install that dependency with pacman, and then run makepkg again.

Now run makepkg and read what it says. It will refuse to build and name a dependency you do not have. Install that dependency with pacman, and then run makepkg again.

The error says "Missing dependency ...". That name is the package you need.

`pacman -S curl` installs it.

makepkg checks every name in depends before it starts anything. That check is the whole point of depends: pacman refuses to hand out a package whose requirements are not met, so nobody ends up with a broken install.

pieces.label: Building a package the proper way — task: Build the package. Run makepkg in the directory that holds the PKGBUILD and watch it finish.

Build the package. Run makepkg in the directory that holds the PKGBUILD and watch it finish.

makepkg reads the PKGBUILD in the directory you are standing in. If it says "PKGBUILD does not exist", you are in the wrong place.

`cd ~/hello` first, then `makepkg`.

A built package is a single file — hello-1.0.0-any.pkg.tar.zst — that anyone can install with pacman -U, and that contains only what package() put into $pkgdir. That is the difference between a package and a folder of scripts.

pieces.label: Building a package the proper way — task: pkgctl is the current front door to devtools: `pkgctl build` is the one-command version of the clean chroot build — the same work makepkg does, through the modern door. There is a second recipe waiting at ~/greeter. Step into it and build it with pkgctl build.

Same rule as makepkg: the recipe has to be in the directory you are standing in.

pieces.label: Building a package the proper way — the point
pieces.text: You wrote a recipe, watched makepkg refuse it for a missing dependency, installed what it needed, and built the package. Then you built a second one through pkgctl, the modern front door to the same toolkit. What you now know is the shape of every Arch package: a shell script that says what the software is, and a build that does not depend on what happens to be installed on your machine.

pieces.label: The AUR, and the helpers that build it — scenario
pieces.text: There is something in the AUR you want — a font, a terminal client, a small tool — and it is not in the official Arch repositories. The AUR is where Arch users put recipes that nobody has audited, and helpers like yay and paru will fetch and build one for you in a single command. This lab is that AUR, those helpers, and the question that decides what ends up on your ISO.

pieces.label: The AUR, and the helpers that build it — the lesson
pieces.text: The AUR — the Arch User Repository — is a pile of build recipes written by users. Not packages exactly: recipes, the PKGBUILD files that describe how to build a package. When you install something from the AUR, your machine downloads the recipe, builds the package from the source it points at, and hands the result to pacman.

pieces.label: The AUR, and the helpers that build it — What the AUR is
pieces.text:
The AUR holds user-submitted build recipes. They are not official packages and they are not in Arch’s repositories — pacman -Ss will never show them to you. The official repositories are curated, tested and signed by the project. The AUR is whatever anybody felt like submitting, and the maintainers of those recipes are strangers.

A helper such as yay or paru is a wrapper around the workflow. It fetches the recipe, builds it in a clean chroot, and installs the result. That convenience is the whole point, and it is also the reason the recipe deserves a look before you let it run.

pieces.label: The AUR, and the helpers that build it — What "unsupported" actually means
pieces.text:
AUR packages are unsupported. That is not a formality. Nobody guarantees the recipe builds, that it still works with current dependencies, or that the source it points at is the source you think it is. The person who wrote the recipe is a stranger with a shell and your user account, and their PKGBUILD is a script that runs as you.

Unsupported does not mean bad. Plenty of AUR packages are excellent, and some of them are better than anything in the repositories. It means the guarantee is missing, and you are the one carrying the risk. The habit that makes that survivable is simple: read the PKGBUILD before you build it. It is a short file. You are looking for the source URL, the depends list, and any install step that reaches outside the package directory.

pieces.label: The AUR, and the helpers that build it — Reading the recipe is the step people skip
pieces.text: When a helper runs, the first thing it does is download the PKGBUILD. That is your chance to look at it — and the recipe is worth reading even when you trust the helper, because the helper will not read it for you. A recipe that installs something into /etc with a curl pipe to a shell is not doing what its description says.

pieces.label: The AUR, and the helpers that build it — What a helper does not do
pieces.text:
This is the part that matters for this course. A helper installs onto the machine you are standing on. It does not put anything on your ISO.

An ISO is assembled from a profile, and the profile lists packages by name — pacman installs those names while the image is being built. If a package is not in the official repositories, the profile cannot ask for it by name, because the image builder has no way to fetch it. So an AUR package has to be built into a package file and served from a local repository that the profile can see. Build it, serve it, list it. Three steps, in that order.

pieces.label: The AUR, and the helpers that build it — task: Search the AUR. Run `yay -Ss` (or `paru -Ss`) and look at what comes back. Notice how each result is labelled — it does not say core/ or extra/ the way pacman’s own results do.
pieces.text:
Search the AUR. Run `yay -Ss` (or `paru -Ss`) and look at what comes back. Notice how each result is labelled — it does not say core/ or extra/ the way pacman’s own results do.

The helper takes pacman’s search flag, but it searches a different place: the AUR, not the repositories.

`yay -Ss` — the results come back prefixed with aur/.

The AUR is a separate index from the official repositories, and it is worth knowing which one a search is looking at. Everything in it is user-submitted, which is exactly why it deserves a closer look than a package from extra/.

pieces.label: The AUR, and the helpers that build it — task: Now ask pacman about the same thing. Search the official repositories for one of the packages you found in the AUR — `pacman -Ss mono`, say — and see what pacman says.
pieces.text:
Now ask pacman about the same thing. Search the official repositories for one of the packages you found in the AUR — `pacman -Ss mono`, say — and see what pacman says.

Same search word, different tool. `pacman -Ss mono` searches the official repositories only.

Try `pacman -Ss mono`, or `pacman -Qi <name>` for a package you saw in the AUR.

This is the plain meaning of "unofficial": the package is not in the repositories, it is not signed by the project, and no maintainer is on the hook for it. It is a recipe somebody wrote, and it is yours to read before you trust it.

pieces.label: The AUR, and the helpers that build it — task: Install one of the AUR packages with a helper. Watch the output as it goes: the helper downloads the PKGBUILD first, and that file — not the helper’s promise — is what tells you what you are about to run.
pieces.text:
Install one of the AUR packages with a helper. Watch the output as it goes: the helper downloads the PKGBUILD first, and that file — not the helper’s promise — is what tells you what you are about to run.

The helper does the whole workflow for you: fetch the recipe, build it in a clean chroot, install the package.

`yay -S ttf-jetbrains-mono` — pick anything you saw in the search.

The helper turns a pile of shell commands into one. What it does not turn into one is your reading of the recipe it downloaded. The PKGBUILD that came down is the thing to open and read, every time.

pieces.label: The AUR, and the helpers that build it — task: One more thing, and it is the one this course is about. A helper installs on this machine. Your ISO does not get it that way — the image only ever gets what its profile lists, and the profile can only ask for packages that live in a repository the image builder can see. Write that down for yourself in a file called aur-to-iso.txt in your home: what has to happen to an AUR package before it can go on an image.
pieces.text:
One more thing, and it is the one this course is about. A helper installs on this machine. Your ISO does not get it that way — the image only ever gets what its profile lists, and the profile can only ask for packages that live in a repository the image builder can see. Write that down for yourself in a file called aur-to-iso.txt in your home: what has to happen to an AUR package before it can go on an image.

Two steps, in order: first the recipe becomes a package, then that package becomes something the profile can ask for.

Write something like: "build it with makepkg, serve the package from a local repo the profile can see, then list it in the profile".

An ISO is not a snapshot of the machine you built it on. It is the profile, resolved against repositories, at build time. Anything not in a repository the image builder can see simply is not on the image — no matter how many helpers you ran on your own desktop.

pieces.label: The AUR, and the helpers that build it — the point
pieces.text: You found a recipe in the AUR, confirmed that the official repositories never had it, and let a helper build and install it. None of that makes it trustworthy — it makes it convenient. The AUR is unsupported, and the thing that makes that survivable is reading the recipe before you let it run.

pieces.label: Reading a PKGBUILD — scenario
pieces.text: You are handed a PKGBUILD. Not a toy one — a real recipe, from a project that renamed itself and left a few old names behind. Before you can fix it, or judge it, or write your own, you have to be able to read it: what each variable means, and what a wrong value in it costs you. This is that skill, one variable at a time.

pieces.label: Reading a PKGBUILD — the lesson
pieces.text: A PKGBUILD is a shell script that describes a package: what it is, where it comes from, how it is built, and what goes into it. Every assignment in it is a variable with a job. The functions at the bottom are the steps, in order. Reading a recipe is mostly reading these two things, and this lab walks the whole set of them on one real file.

pieces.label: Reading a PKGBUILD — pkgname, and pkgbase
pieces.text: pkgname is the package’s name — the thing pacman will call it, and the first part of the file that comes out. It is an array when one recipe builds several packages, a split package: a shared library and the tools that go with it, say. When that happens, pkgbase names the recipe itself, so the two can be told apart.

pieces.label: Reading a PKGBUILD — pkgver and pkgrel
pieces.text:
pkgver is the upstream version, exactly as the software’s own authors number it: letters, numbers, dots. No hyphens — pacman compares this string to decide what is newer, and the hyphen is its own separator.

pkgrel is the packaging release: 1, 2, 3. It resets to 1 whenever pkgver changes, and climbs when only the recipe changed. Version is the software; release is the packaging of it.

pieces.label: Reading a PKGBUILD — pkgdesc, arch, url, license
pieces.text:
pkgdesc is one short line saying what the package is. It is what pacman -Ss shows the world, so it is read by people deciding whether to install something.

arch says which architectures the package builds for: x86_64, aarch64, or any for the things that run anywhere — scripts, fonts, wallpapers.

url is the software’s home on the web.

license is its licence, from the standard set: GPL, MIT, Apache, and so on, or custom when nothing else fits. It is not decoration. Shipping a package under the wrong licence is a legal problem.

pieces.label: Reading a PKGBUILD — depends, makedepends, checkdepends, optdepends
pieces.text:
depends is what must be installed for the package to RUN. Pacman enforces it: if the list is wrong, the package installs and then does not work.

makedepends is what must be present to BUILD it, and is not needed to run it: compilers, headers, build tools. The difference between depends and makedepends is the difference between the kitchen and the table — the kitchen tools stay in the kitchen.

checkdepends is what the test suite needs while check() runs.

optdepends is optional extras, each with a few words on what it adds. Pacman suggests these; it never forces them.

pieces.label: Reading a PKGBUILD — provides, conflicts, replaces, backup
pieces.text:
provides, conflicts and replaces are the package’s relationships with others: what it can stand in for, what it cannot live alongside, and what it supersedes.

backup lists the files pacman will not silently overwrite when it upgrades something — usually configuration under /etc. It saves a copy with a .pacnew suffix and lets you merge it yourself.

pieces.label: Reading a PKGBUILD — options, install, source, sha256sums, validpgpkeys
pieces.text:
options holds build switches, most of them negations: !strip, !docs, !emptydirs. You mostly meet them when something needs an exception.

install names a scriptlet file with instructions pacman runs at install, upgrade and remove time.

source says where everything comes from: tarball URLs, local files, or a git repository — with the branch or the commit pinned in the source string itself, so the build cannot drift.

sha256sums (or b2sums) is one checksum per source, in the same order, proving the download is the file the recipe was written against. SKIP exists, mainly for git sources — and choosing it is a decision, not a shortcut.

validpgpkeys lists the fingerprints allowed to sign the sources, for the projects whose tarballs are signed.

pieces.label: Reading a PKGBUILD — The four functions
pieces.text:
prepare() unpacks the source and applies any patches. build() compiles it. check() runs the test suite. package() lays the finished files into the package root — $pkgdir, never the real filesystem.

For a split package, there is one package() per pkgname, so each output gets its own set of files.

pieces.label: Reading a PKGBUILD — task: Find the package’s own name. It is near the top of the file, and one line further down still carries the old name — the install scriptlet line. Put the right file name there: install=<name>.install.
pieces.text:
Find the package’s own name. It is near the top of the file, and one line further down still carries the old name — the install scriptlet line. Put the right file name there: install=<name>.install.

pkgname is the first assignment in the file. The scriptlet file has to carry that name.

install=greet.install

pkgname is not decoration: it becomes the package’s name in pacman’s database, the file name of the built package, and the name every scriptlet, conflict and dependency entry has to agree with.

pieces.label: Reading a PKGBUILD — task: Find what the description should say. The pkgdesc line still describes the old package — the one-line description the repositories should show is written in the notes at the top of the file. Put it in the pkgdesc line.
pieces.text:
Find what the description should say. The pkgdesc line still describes the old package — the one-line description the repositories should show is written in the notes at the top of the file. Put it in the pkgdesc line.

Scroll to the top. The previous maintainer left the wording in the comment block.

pkgdesc="A tiny command line tool that prints a friendly greeting"

pkgdesc is what pacman -Ss prints under the package name. It is the only thing a user reads before deciding whether to install something, so it has to describe the software that is actually in the package.

pieces.label: Reading a PKGBUILD — task: Find the licence. The licence line claims one thing; the notes at the top of the file say what upstream actually uses. Set the licence array to the truth.
pieces.text:
Find the licence. The licence line claims one thing; the notes at the top of the file say what upstream actually uses. Set the licence array to the truth.

The previous maintainer wrote the licence down in the notes at the top of the file.

license=('MIT')

The licence tells the people who install the package what they are allowed to do with it. Getting it wrong is not a small mistake, and nobody downstream will catch it for you.

pieces.label: Reading a PKGBUILD — task: Find what has to be present to build this but not to run it. One of the names in makedepends belongs in depends instead — it is already there. Take it out of makedepends and leave the build tools alone.
pieces.text:
Find what has to be present to build this but not to run it. One of the names in makedepends belongs in depends instead — it is already there. Take it out of makedepends and leave the build tools alone.

Look for a name that appears in both lists. The one that appears in both is the one that does not belong in makedepends.

makedepends=('gcc' 'make')

The difference between depends and makedepends is the difference between the kitchen and the table. Put a runtime library in makedepends and every machine that installs the package carries a build tool it will never use; leave it out of depends and the package installs broken.

pieces.label: Reading a PKGBUILD — task: Find the checksum list. Right now the source is a tarball and its checksum is SKIP — which means nobody checked the download. The real sha256 for that tarball is written in the notes at the top of the file. Put it in the list.
pieces.text:
Find the checksum list. Right now the source is a tarball and its checksum is SKIP — which means nobody checked the download. The real sha256 for that tarball is written in the notes at the top of the file. Put it in the list.

The notes at the top of the file record the sha256 of the upstream tarball, one long line of hex.

sha256sums=('9f2c1e7b4d8a6035c1e2f7a9d4b6c8e0f2a5b7d9c1e3f5a7b9d1c3e5f7a9b1d3')

The checksum is what proves the file you downloaded is the file the recipe was written against. SKIP is a decision, and for a plain tarball there is no good reason to make it — for git sources, where there is no fixed file to hash, there is.

pieces.label: Reading a PKGBUILD — task: Find where the source comes from. The source line still points at the old project’s directory. The tarball for this package lives under https://example.org/greet/ — and the file name has to carry the version, so use $pkgver in the URL.
pieces.text:
Find where the source comes from. The source line still points at the old project’s directory. The tarball for this package lives under https://example.org/greet/ — and the file name has to carry the version, so use $pkgver in the URL.

Compare the source line with the url line. One of them was updated when the project was renamed.

source=("https://example.org/greet/greet-$pkgver.tar.gz")

The source line is where the package comes from and the checksum line is what proves it arrived intact. Get the URL wrong and the build fetches somebody else’s file, or nothing at all.

pieces.label: Reading a PKGBUILD — task: Find the function that lays the built files into the package. It is doing it wrong: it installs straight into /usr/bin and /etc, which would write to your live system. Everything a package installs has to go under $pkgdir — the directory that becomes / when the package is installed.
pieces.text:
Find the function that lays the built files into the package. It is doing it wrong: it installs straight into /usr/bin and /etc, which would write to your live system. Everything a package installs has to go under $pkgdir — the directory that becomes / when the package is installed.

Look at the two install lines inside package(). The destination is wrong in both of them.

package() never touches your system; it assembles a directory tree that pacman later copies into /. Writing to /usr/bin during a build pollutes the machine you built on and puts files in the package that nobody asked for.

pieces.label: Reading a PKGBUILD — task: One step is missing entirely. The notes say the tarball needs patching before it will build — and unpacking and patching is what prepare() is for. Add a prepare() function.
Reading a PKGBUILD — the point
pieces.text: You read a real PKGBUILD and found every stale spot in it: the old name in the scriptlet line, the description that still described the old package, the wrong licence, the runtime dependency hiding in makedepends, the skipped checksum, the source URL pointing at the old project, the install step writing to the real filesystem, and the missing prepare().

pieces.label: Writing a PKGBUILD — scenario
pieces.text: There is a small program that needs a recipe. Notefile: a tiny command line notepad that appends a line to a note file and can sync the note to a remote server. It has an upstream release, a licence, a tarball and a build system, and none of that means anything to pacman until somebody writes the PKGBUILD that says all of it. That somebody is you.

pieces.label: Writing a PKGBUILD — the lesson
pieces.text: A PKGBUILD is a shell script, and every assignment in it is a variable with a job. Fill them in honestly and the packaging tools can do the rest; leave one of them wrong and the failure is quiet — a package that installs broken, a version that never updates, a licence that is not yours to give. This lab fills in one, variable by variable, and checks each one on its own.

pieces.label: Writing a PKGBUILD — The program you are packaging
pieces.text:
Notefile is a tiny command line notepad. It appends a line to a note file, and with -s it syncs the note to a remote server over HTTPS, so it needs curl at run time.

Upstream calls the release 1.4.0 and licenses it MIT. The project page is https://example.org/notefile, and the tarball is https://example.org/notefile/notefile-1.4.0.tar.gz. It builds with make and gcc, its tests want shunit2, and bash is an optional extra that adds tab completion.

pkgname is the package’s name; pkgver is the upstream version, exactly as its authors number it — letters, numbers, dots, and no hyphens, because pacman uses the hyphen to separate the version from the packaging release. pkgrel is that packaging release: 1, 2, 3, counting up while only the recipe changes and resetting to 1 whenever pkgver changes.
