pieces.text: depends is what must be installed for the package to RUN, and pacman enforces it. makedepends is what must be present to BUILD it and is not needed to run it: the compiler, the headers, make. The same name in both lists is a mistake — the kitchen tools stay in the kitchen. checkdepends is what the test suite needs while check() runs, and optdepends is optional extras, each with a few words on what it adds.

pieces.label: Writing a PKGBUILD — Sources and checksums
pieces.text: source says where everything comes from: tarball URLs, local files, or a git repository with the branch or commit pinned in the source string itself. sha256sums holds one checksum per source, in the same order, proving the download is the file the recipe was written against. SKIP exists, mainly for git sources — and choosing it is a decision, not a shortcut.

pieces.label: Writing a PKGBUILD — The four functions
pieces.text: prepare() unpacks the source and applies any patches. build() compiles it. check() runs the tests. package() lays the built files into the package root — $pkgdir, and only $pkgdir. $pkgdir becomes / when the package is installed, so a package() that writes to /usr/bin is not building a package, it is modifying your machine.

pieces.label: Writing a PKGBUILD — task: Give the package its name. pkgname is the name pacman will know it by, and the first part of the file that comes out.
pieces.text:
Give the package its name. pkgname is the name pacman will know it by, and the first part of the file that comes out.

It goes on the line that says pkgname=, in lower case and with no spaces.

pkgname=notefile

The name is how the package is known for its whole life: in pacman’s database, in the built file’s name, and in every dependency entry that refers to it.

pieces.label: Writing a PKGBUILD — task: Say which version this is. pkgver is the upstream version — the version the software’s own authors number it — and pkgrel is the packaging release, counting up from 1.
pieces.text:
Say which version this is. pkgver is the upstream version — the version the software’s own authors number it — and pkgrel is the packaging release, counting up from 1.

pacman compares pkgver to decide what is newer, so the hyphen is reserved: the version cannot contain one.

pkgver=1.4.0 and pkgrel=1 — this is the first packaging of it.

Version is the software; release is the packaging of it. Get the hyphen rule wrong and pacman compares versions wrongly, and users never receive the update you made.

pieces.label: Writing a PKGBUILD — task: Write the description: one short line saying what the package is. This is the line pacman -Ss shows the world.
pieces.text:
Write the description: one short line saying what the package is. This is the line pacman -Ss shows the world.

It is a single line, in the pkgdesc= assignment, and it should be short enough to read in a search result.

pkgdesc="A tiny command line notepad that syncs notes to a server"

pkgdesc is the only thing somebody reads before deciding to install something. Vague or missing, and people install the wrong thing or nothing at all.

pieces.label: Writing a PKGBUILD — task: Say which architectures this builds for. If the program is a script or a font and does not care about the machine, there is a value for exactly that.
pieces.text:
Say which architectures this builds for. If the program is a script or a font and does not care about the machine, there is a value for exactly that.

Three answers: x86_64, aarch64, and the one for anything that runs everywhere.

arch=('any') — a notepad script does not care what the CPU is.

arch tells pacman whether a package can be installed on this machine at all. Getting it wrong means either a package nobody can install, or one that gets installed where it cannot run.

pieces.label: Writing a PKGBUILD — task: Point at the software’s home on the web.
pieces.text:
Point at the software’s home on the web.

It goes on the url= line, and it starts with https://.

url="https://example.org/notefile"

url is where a person goes to find out what a package is, report a problem, or read the changelog. It is the link that makes the rest of the recipe checkable.

pieces.label: Writing a PKGBUILD — task: Record the licence, taken from the standard set. If nothing fits, there is a value for that too.
pieces.text:
Record the licence, taken from the standard set. If nothing fits, there is a value for that too.

It is an array, like arch and depends: license=(MIT).

license=('MIT') — notefile is MIT licensed.

The licence says what the people who install the package are allowed to do with it. Getting it wrong is a legal problem for you and for everyone downstream.

pieces.label: Writing a PKGBUILD — task: List what has to be installed for this package to RUN. Pacman enforces this list, so if you get it wrong the package installs broken.
pieces.text:
List what has to be installed for this package to RUN. Pacman enforces this list, so if you get it wrong the package installs broken.

depends is an array of package names. Notefile syncs over HTTPS, so one thing belongs here.

depends=('curl')

depends is a promise pacman keeps on your behalf: when the package installs, its requirements are already there. Leave a runtime dependency out and the failure lands on the user, not on you.

pieces.label: Writing a PKGBUILD — task: List what has to be present to BUILD this package but not to run it: the compiler, the headers, make. The same name must not appear in both lists.
pieces.text:
List what has to be present to BUILD this package but not to run it: the compiler, the headers, make. The same name must not appear in both lists.

makedepends is the kitchen; depends is the table. A name that appears in both is the mistake.

makedepends=('gcc' 'make')

The difference between depends and makedepends is the difference between the kitchen and the table. Put a runtime library in makedepends and every machine that installs the package carries build tools it will never use.

pieces.label: Writing a PKGBUILD — task: Say where the source comes from, and give one checksum per source, in the same order. The checksum is what proves the download is the file the recipe was written against.
pieces.text:
Say where the source comes from, and give one checksum per source, in the same order. The checksum is what proves the download is the file the recipe was written against.

source is an array of URLs; sha256sums is an array of checksums with exactly as many entries as source has.

source=("https://example.org/notefile/notefile-1.4.0.tar.gz") and one 64-character hex checksum beside it.

The URL says where the code comes from and the checksum says it is the code you expected. SKIP is a decision — fine for git sources, hard to defend for a plain tarball.

pieces.label: Writing a PKGBUILD — task: Write the four functions. prepare() unpacks and patches, build() compiles, check() runs the tests, package() lays the built files into the package root — and the package root is $pkgdir, never the real filesystem.
pieces.text:
Write the four functions. prepare() unpacks and patches, build() compiles, check() runs the tests, package() lays the built files into the package root — and the package root is $pkgdir, never the real filesystem.

The install line inside package() has to point inside $pkgdir, so that the file lands in the package and not on this machine.

install -Dm755 notefile "$pkgdir/usr/bin/notefile" — the destination is under $pkgdir.

A package is what package() collects, and nothing else. If package() writes to /usr/bin, the build has modified the machine it ran on and the package is missing the file it promised.

pieces.label: Writing a PKGBUILD — task: Put it all together and build it. With every variable filled in and every function present, makepkg turns this PKGBUILD into a package file: notefile-<version>-<arch>.pkg.tar.zst. The terminal under the editor sees the file you are writing — run makepkg there.
pieces.text:
Put it all together and build it. With every variable filled in and every function present, makepkg turns this PKGBUILD into a package file: notefile-<version>-<arch>.pkg.tar.zst. The terminal under the editor sees the file you are writing — run makepkg there.

makepkg reads the PKGBUILD in the directory you are standing in, checks the depends list, and writes the package file next to it.

cd to the directory holding this PKGBUILD, then makepkg.

This is the payoff: a recipe that is right in every variable produces a package other people can install with one command, and produces the same package on their machine as on yours.

pieces.label: Writing a PKGBUILD — the point
pieces.text: You wrote a complete PKGBUILD — name, version, release, description, architecture, home page, licence, the two dependency lists kept separate, the source with a checksum beside it, and the four functions with package() filling $pkgdir and nothing else. Every one of those variables is a promise to the person who installs your package.

pieces.label: What a profile is made of — scenario
pieces.text: Every Linux distribution you have ever booted was assembled from a list of files and a list of packages. Arch ships the tool that does this — archiso — and the recipe it reads is called a profile. A profile is not a script and it is not a config file you point at: it is a directory, and that directory *is* the recipe. This lab is about learning to read one.

pieces.label: What a profile is made of — the lesson
pieces.text: archiso takes a profile — a directory — and turns it into a bootable ISO image. Every profile has the same five parts. `profiledef.sh` describes the image itself: its name, its label, where its files sit on the disc, which boot loaders to bake in. `packages.<arch>` lists the packages that go into the image, one per line. `pacman.conf` says where those packages are fetched from. `airootfs/` is a directory of files that get copied onto the image's own root filesystem. And the boot loader directories — `grub/`, `syslinux/`, `efiboot/` — configure the menu you see when the machine starts. Two more variables exist and do not matter yet: `buildmodes` (how to build the thing) and `bootmodes` (which boot loaders to include). Boot modes get their own lab.

pieces.label: What a profile is made of — The shape of the directory
pieces.text:
This is the profile you are looking at. Five things, and every one of them has a job:

profiledef.sh — the identity of the image. Name, label, version, install directory, boot loaders.

packages.x86_64 — the contents. One package per line. Blank lines and lines starting with a # are ignored.

pacman.conf — the source. Which mirrors the packages are fetched from while the image is being built.

airootfs/ — the overlay. Everything in here is copied onto the image's root filesystem before the packages are installed.

grub/ and syslinux/ — the menus. One directory per boot loader.

pieces.label: What a profile is made of — Where the filename comes from
pieces.text: The image is called <iso_name>-<iso_version>-<arch>.iso. The arch part comes from the `arch` variable, which also picks the package list: packages.x86_64. The volume label — the name the disc is given inside a file manager — is a separate thing entirely, and it is `iso_label`.

pieces.label: What a profile is made of — task: Open `profiledef.sh`. The image is still called after somebody else's project. Change `iso_name` so the image is named after yours: vesper.
pieces.text:
Open `profiledef.sh`. The image is still called after somebody else's project. Change `iso_name` so the image is named after yours: vesper.

Look in profiledef.sh for the line that starts with `iso_name=`. It is the first assignment in the file.

The line should read: iso_name="vesper"

The image filename is built from iso_name, iso_version and the architecture, so iso_name is the half of the filename people recognise. Getting it right means the artefact is named after the flavour rather than after the template it started from — which matters the moment more than one build exists.

pieces.label: What a profile is made of — task: Still in `profiledef.sh`: `install_dir` names the directory the image's files live in on the disc. Set it to vesper. Remember the rule — lowercase letters and digits only, nothing else.
pieces.text:
Still in `profiledef.sh`: `install_dir` names the directory the image's files live in on the disc. Set it to vesper. Remember the rule — lowercase letters and digits only, nothing else.

The rule is not "no spaces" — it is stricter. Only [a-z0-9] is allowed.

The line should read: install_dir="vesper"

install_dir is the folder your kernel, initramfs and root filesystem are mounted from on the disc. The boot loaders are told about it at build time by the %INSTALL_DIR% placeholder, so the value and the menus are always in step. The character restriction is not cosmetic: the name ends up in boot parameters and in paths that several different tools have to agree about, and a name with case in it has bitten people on case-insensitive filesystems.

pieces.label: What a profile is made of — task: The volume label is a different thing from the filename: it is the name the disc is given inside a file manager, and it is set by `iso_label` in `profiledef.sh`. Set it to VESPER_202611.
pieces.text:
The volume label is a different thing from the filename: it is the name the disc is given inside a file manager, and it is set by `iso_label` in `profiledef.sh`. Set it to VESPER_202611.

The label and the name are two different variables. You want `iso_label="VESPER_202611"` — all capitals.

The line should read: iso_label="VESPER_202611"

A volume label is what shows up in a file manager, in a disk utility, and on the boot screen of some machines. It is the first thing that tells somebody which image they have in their hand, and it is limited to uppercase and to 32 characters because of the filesystem it lives in.

pieces.label: What a profile is made of — task: The profile does not say which architecture it is for. Add `arch="x86_64"` to `profiledef.sh`. That one value decides which package list is read — the one called `packages.x86_64` — and make sure that list names the kernel.
pieces.text:
The profile does not say which architecture it is for. Add `arch="x86_64"` to `profiledef.sh`. That one value decides which package list is read — the one called `packages.x86_64` — and make sure that list names the kernel.

One line in profiledef.sh, near the other assignments. And in packages.x86_64, a line that says exactly `linux` — no trailing words, because the whole line is the package name.

arch="x86_64" in profiledef.sh, and a line reading `linux` in packages.x86_64.

The package list is the contents of the image, and the arch variable is how the profile finds it: packages.${arch}. Setting it explicitly means the profile builds the same thing on every machine, instead of producing an aarch64 image because you happened to be on one.

pieces.label: What a profile is made of — task: The `airootfs/` directory is the overlay: everything in it is copied onto the image's own root filesystem. It already holds `airootfs/etc/motd` — the message printed the first time somebody logs in. Rewrite it so it greets the person as Vesper.
pieces.text:
The `airootfs/` directory is the overlay: everything in it is copied onto the image's own root filesystem. It already holds `airootfs/etc/motd` — the message printed the first time somebody logs in. Rewrite it so it greets the person as Vesper.

The path inside the profile is airootfs/etc/motd. On the image it becomes /etc/motd — the overlay keeps the same shape as the root filesystem.

Put a line like "Welcome to Vesper." in airootfs/etc/motd.

The overlay is how you put your own files into the image without packaging anything. The path you write in the profile is the path the file has on the image, so airootfs/etc/motd becomes /etc/motd. It is the cheapest possible customisation: a file, copied in, that says your name.

pieces.label: What a profile is made of — task: Right now the profile does not say where the packages come from. Point it at its own configuration file: add `pacman_conf="pacman.conf"` to `profiledef.sh`.
pieces.text:
Right now the profile does not say where the packages come from. Point it at its own configuration file: add `pacman_conf="pacman.conf"` to `profiledef.sh`.

One more assignment in profiledef.sh, naming the file that is already there.

The line should read: pacman_conf="pacman.conf"

pacman_conf names the pacman configuration that governs the build. Leaving it out is the single easiest way to get an image that is not reproducible: the build silently inherits the build machine's mirrors. Pointing it at the profile's own file is what makes the recipe mean the same thing everywhere.

pieces.label: What a profile is made of — task: Last part: the boot menus. The UEFI menu lives in `grub/grub.cfg`, and the entry in it still calls itself "Arch Linux". Rename that menu entry so it says Vesper.
pieces.text:
Last part: the boot menus. The UEFI menu lives in `grub/grub.cfg`, and the entry in it still calls itself "Arch Linux". Rename that menu entry so it says Vesper.

Find the word menuentry in grub/grub.cfg. The name of the image is the text in double quotes right after it.

Something like: menuentry "Vesper Linux (%ARCH%, ${archiso_platform})" — keep the rest of the line exactly as it is.

The bootloader configuration is the last part of the profile, and it is the part a user actually sees. grub/ serves UEFI machines and syslinux/ serves BIOS machines; each is a directory of plain configuration files. A profile that names a boot mode has to have the matching directory, and the menu entries in it are the same template mechanism everywhere: %INSTALL_DIR% and friends are filled in at build time.

pieces.label: What a profile is made of — the point
pieces.text: You have read a profile the way an archiso maintainer reads one: five parts, each with one job. Everything else in this course hangs off that shape — the package list, the overlay and the boot menus are each one of those five parts seen from a different side.

pieces.label: Packages and pacman configuration — scenario
pieces.text: A profile with the right shape still builds the wrong image if the package list is wrong or the mirrors are wrong. And the failure is quiet: the build succeeds, the ISO boots, and six months later somebody asks why their machine pulled its packages from a mirror the project never chose. This lab is about the two files that decide what is inside the image and where it came from.

pieces.label: Packages and pacman configuration — the lesson
pieces.text:
The file `packages.x86_64` is a pacman list — one package per line, exactly the kind of list you would hand to `pacman -S`. A line starting with # is a comment and is ignored, and so are blank lines. Two packages are not optional: `mkinitcpio`, which builds the initramfs, and `mkinitcpio-archiso`, which teaches that initramfs how to find the root filesystem on the disc. Without the second one you have no bootable image, whatever else is right.

The pacman configuration decides where those packages come from. Here is the part that catches everybody: there are TWO pacman configurations, and they are different files. The profile's `pacman.conf` governs the BUILD — mkarchiso reads it and pacstrap uses it to fill the image. The file at `airootfs/etc/pacman.conf` is the one inside the RUNNING IMAGE — it is what pacman reads once somebody boots your ISO and installs something. They can point at different mirrors, and if they do, the image you tested is not the image people get.

pieces.label: Packages and pacman configuration — The rule about relative Include
pieces.text: pacman resolves a relative `Include` against the directory you are standing in when you run it — not against the directory the file containing the Include lives in. So a profile whose pacman.conf says `Include = mirrorlist` builds happily if you happen to be standing in a directory that has a mirrorlist in it, and fails if you are not. A profile must not depend on the directory somebody happened to be in, so the servers are written out in full.

pieces.label: Packages and pacman configuration — What the two configurations are for
pieces.text:
Build time: the profile's pacman.conf. This decides which mirror your packages are downloaded from while the image is assembled.

Run time: airootfs/etc/pacman.conf. This decides which mirror the running image fetches from later, when somebody installs a package inside it.

The build one is a file in your profile. The runtime one is a file you drop into the overlay, and it is the overlay that puts it inside the image.

pieces.label: Packages and pacman configuration — task: Add `nano` to the package list. The list is a pacman list: one package per line, and the line is nothing but the package name.
pieces.text:
Add `nano` to the package list. The list is a pacman list: one package per line, and the line is nothing but the package name.

Look at the shape of the other entries. A package is a line containing just the name.

Add a line reading exactly: nano

The package list is the contents of the image, and it is handed to pacman almost verbatim. That is why the format is strict: one name per line, nothing else. A trailing comment on the same line is not a comment to pacman — it is part of the name.

pieces.label: Packages and pacman configuration — task: Take `vim` out of the image. This time, remove the line entirely rather than commenting it out.
pieces.text:
Take `vim` out of the image. This time, remove the line entirely rather than commenting it out.

Find the line that says vim and delete it, rather than putting a # in front.

The line "vim" should be gone from the file entirely.

Commenting a package out and deleting it have the same effect on the build — both stop it being installed — but they mean different things to the next person who reads the profile. A deleted line says "we do not want this". A commented line says "we had this once".

pieces.label: Packages and pacman configuration — task: Now do it the other way round: keep `tree` in the file, but stop it being installed. Put a `#` in front of the line.
pieces.text:
Now do it the other way round: keep `tree` in the file, but stop it being installed. Put a `#` in front of the line.

The # goes at the very start of the line, before the package name.

The line should read: #tree

A # at the start of a line turns a package into a comment. Archiso skips comment lines and blank lines, so the package is not installed — which is how you keep a note about a package you tried without carrying it into every build.

pieces.label: Packages and pacman configuration — task: Two packages in this list are not optional. `mkinitcpio` is here; `mkinitcpio-archiso` is missing. Add it, because without it the image does not boot.
pieces.text:
Two packages in this list are not optional. `mkinitcpio` is here; `mkinitcpio-archiso` is missing. Add it, because without it the image does not boot.

It goes in the list like any other package. Its name has a hyphen in it.

Add a line reading exactly: mkinitcpio-archiso

mkinitcpio builds the initramfs — the small filesystem the kernel unpacks into before the real root filesystem is available. mkinitcpio-archiso is the archiso-specific part of that: it knows about the medium. Its absence is the classic archiso failure, and it is quiet — the image builds fine and fails at boot.

pieces.label: Packages and pacman configuration — task: In the build's `pacman.conf`, the signature policy is commented out. Write it out: `SigLevel = Required DatabaseOptional`.
pieces.text:
In the build's `pacman.conf`, the signature policy is commented out. Write it out: `SigLevel = Required DatabaseOptional`.

Find the line in pacman.conf that starts with #SigLevel and take the # off.

The line should read: SigLevel = Required DatabaseOptional

SigLevel tells pacman how much signature checking to do. Required means a package must be signed by a key in the trusted keyring; DatabaseOptional means the repository databases may be unsigned. Writing the policy out in the profile means the build behaves the same way on every machine, instead of depending on what the build host happens to have configured.

pieces.label: Packages and pacman configuration — task: The build's `pacman.conf` pulls its servers in with `Include = mirrorlist`. That does not work in a profile: pacman resolves a relative Include against the directory you are standing in, not the directory the file lives in. So the same profile builds from one directory and fails from another. Write the servers out in full instead — a `Server = https://…` line under [core] and one under [extra].
pieces.text:
The build's `pacman.conf` pulls its servers in with `Include = mirrorlist`. That does not work in a profile: pacman resolves a relative Include against the directory you are standing in, not the directory the file lives in. So the same profile builds from one directory and fails from another. Write the servers out in full instead — a `Server = https://…` line under [core] and one under [extra].

Delete the Include lines and put a Server line under each repository heading. The $repo and $arch in the URL are variables pacman fills in.

Under [core]: Server = https://geo.mirror.pkgbuild.com/$repo/os/$arch — and the same under [extra].

A relative Include makes the profile depend on where it is being built from. The same profile that built on a machine with a mirrorlist in its working directory fails on the next machine, and the error is about a missing file rather than about the profile, which is a miserable thing to debug. Writing the servers out in full makes the profile hermetic: it says where it wants to fetch from, and it says the same thing wherever the build runs.

pieces.label: Packages and pacman configuration — task: The running image has its own pacman configuration, at `airootfs/etc/pacman.conf`, and right now it names a different mirror from the build. Make it name the same mirror the build uses — copy the Server lines from `pacman.conf` into it.
pieces.text:
The running image has its own pacman configuration, at `airootfs/etc/pacman.conf`, and right now it names a different mirror from the build. Make it name the same mirror the build uses — copy the Server lines from `pacman.conf` into it.

Open both files side by side. Copy the Server lines from the build's pacman.conf into the image's pacman.conf.

The runtime file should end up with the same Server = https://… lines under [core] and [extra] as the build file has.

The build configuration and the runtime configuration answer two different questions — where do the image's own packages come from, and where do packages installed later come from — but if they disagree, the image is split-brained: it was assembled from one mirror and configured to pull from another. That is how a project ends up shipping a build it never tested, and how a mirror gets traffic nobody asked it to have.

pieces.label: Packages and pacman configuration — the point
pieces.text: You now know where an image gets its contents and where it gets its sources — and that there are two of each, not one. The package list is a pacman list, comments are how you talk to the next person, mkinitcpio-archiso is not optional, and a profile that inherits its mirrors from the directory it was built in is not a profile anybody can reproduce.

pieces.label: The airootfs overlay — scenario
pieces.text: You want the image to greet people by name, to ship a script of your own, and to have a password file nobody else can read. None of that needs a package. All of it is one directory: airootfs/. This is the cheapest customisation archiso offers, and it comes with three rules that are worth learning properly the first time rather than the third time.

pieces.label: The airootfs overlay — the lesson
pieces.text:
`airootfs/` is an overlay. The whole directory is copied onto the image's root filesystem, and the path inside the overlay is the path on the image — airootfs/etc/motd becomes /etc/motd.

The copying happens BEFORE the packages are installed. That single fact explains three things. First, you can drop any file you like onto the image without packaging anything. Second, the copy does not carry permissions or ownership: everything arrives as mode 644, owned by root — so a script you drop in cannot be run, and the only way to give it an executable bit is the `file_permissions` array in profiledef.sh. Third, a file that a package also owns gets replaced by that package, because the package is installed afterwards and wins. There are exceptions — /etc/pacman.conf is one of them — and the exception is that pacman treats it as a backup file: it leaves your copy alone and puts the packaged one beside it as /etc/pacman.conf.pacnew.

pieces.label: The airootfs overlay — Why the copy is not a copy
pieces.text:
archiso copies the overlay into the work directory and then installs the packages on top of it. It does not preserve what your files looked like on your disk: modes are reset to 644 for files and 755 for directories, and everything is owned by root.

So if you want a file with a different owner or mode, you cannot do it by setting it in your working directory. You list it in profiledef.sh under file_permissions, as an associative array of path to owner UID, owner GID and mode: ["/etc/shadow"]="0:0:400".

pieces.label: The airootfs overlay — Which files the packages take back
pieces.text:
If you drop a file at a path that a package also owns, the package wins — it is installed after your copy, and it overwrites it.

Some files are exempt. A package can declare a file a backup file, and pacman then refuses to overwrite a version that is already on disk; it puts the packaged version alongside it with a .pacnew suffix. /etc/pacman.conf is one of these, which is exactly why a profile can carry its own pacman configuration in the overlay.

pieces.label: The airootfs overlay — task: Put a file of your own on the image. Write `airootfs/etc/vesper-release` so that it says something like `vesper 2026.11.10` — a release file, so somebody inside the running system can tell what they booted.
pieces.text:
Put a file of your own on the image. Write `airootfs/etc/vesper-release` so that it says something like `vesper 2026.11.10` — a release file, so somebody inside the running system can tell what they booted.

The file is open above, empty. Type into it. The path in the profile is airootfs/etc/vesper-release; on the image it is /etc/vesper-release.

A single line such as: vesper 2026.11.10

This is the overlay doing the one thing it is best at: putting a file of yours on the image without packaging anything. The path inside the overlay is the path on the image, so the directory structure you see in the profile is the directory structure of the finished system.

pieces.label: The airootfs overlay — task: The message a user reads the first time they log in is `/etc/motd`. Yours still says "Welcome to the image". Rewrite `airootfs/etc/motd` so it welcomes them to Vesper.
pieces.text:
The message a user reads the first time they log in is `/etc/motd`. Yours still says "Welcome to the image". Rewrite `airootfs/etc/motd` so it welcomes them to Vesper.

Change the first line so it says Welcome to Vesper.

Something like: Welcome to Vesper — a live image of your own making.

The motd is the cheapest personality a distribution has. It costs one file in the overlay, it survives every rebuild, and it is the difference between an image that looks like Arch and an image that looks like yours.

pieces.label: The airootfs overlay — task: Write a script. It belongs at `airootfs/usr/local/bin/hello`, so on the image it will be /usr/local/bin/hello. It needs a shebang line — the first line of the file, saying which shell runs it — and it should print a greeting that mentions Vesper.
pieces.text:
Write a script. It belongs at `airootfs/usr/local/bin/hello`, so on the image it will be /usr/local/bin/hello. It needs a shebang line — the first line of the file, saying which shell runs it — and it should print a greeting that mentions Vesper.

The first line of the file starts with #! and names a shell. The rest is ordinary shell.

Something like: #!/usr/bin/env bash — then an echo line that mentions Vesper.

A shebang is not a comment. It is the kernel's instruction sheet: the first two bytes of an executable tell the kernel which program to hand the file to. It is the one line that turns a text file into a program, and nothing else in the file substitutes for it.

pieces.label: The airootfs overlay — task: The script is still not runnable, and the overlay cannot fix that by itself: files copied out of airootfs/ arrive as 644 — readable, not executable. Give it the executable bit in `profiledef.sh`, under `file_permissions`. It should end up as 755.
pieces.text:
The script is still not runnable, and the overlay cannot fix that by itself: files copied out of airootfs/ arrive as 644 — readable, not executable. Give it the executable bit in `profiledef.sh`, under `file_permissions`. It should end up as 755.

Look at the file_permissions array in profiledef.sh. It is an associative array: a path in square brackets, then the mode after an equals sign.

Inside file_permissions=( ... ), add: ["/usr/local/bin/hello"]="0:0:755"

The overlay copy deliberately throws away ownership and permissions — files become 644 and directories 755, all owned by root — because a profile is usually a git checkout, and git does not carry those things between machines. The consequence is that a script in the overlay cannot be run until file_permissions says so. The three fields are owner UID, owner GID and mode; 0:0 is root:root, and 755 is the usual mode for something everybody may run.

pieces.label: The airootfs overlay — task: The same mechanism, for a file that must not be world-readable. `/etc/shadow` holds the hashed passwords. List it in `file_permissions` in `profiledef.sh` with the mode 400.
pieces.text:
The same mechanism, for a file that must not be world-readable. `/etc/shadow` holds the hashed passwords. List it in `file_permissions` in `profiledef.sh` with the mode 400.

Same array, same shape as the one you just added. The path is /etc/shadow and the mode is 400.

Add: ["/etc/shadow"]="0:0:400"

644 on a password file means every account on the system can read the hashes, which is exactly what you do not want. 400 is the mode for root-only-and-readable. Setting it here means it is right on every build, including the ones somebody else runs from their own checkout of your profile.

pieces.label: The airootfs overlay — task: One more overlay file. Write `airootfs/etc/pacman.conf` — the pacman configuration for the RUNNING image — with a first line that reads `# Vesper runtime pacman config`, and a `[core]` section underneath with a `Server = https://…` line naming your mirror.
pieces.text:
One more overlay file. Write `airootfs/etc/pacman.conf` — the pacman configuration for the RUNNING image — with a first line that reads `# Vesper runtime pacman config`, and a `[core]` section underneath with a `Server = https://…` line naming your mirror.

The file is open above and empty. A comment starts with a #. Under [core], a Server line gives the mirror.

Something like: # Vesper runtime pacman config — then [core] and a Server = https://… line.

You might expect the pacman package to overwrite this file, because the package is installed after your copy is laid down — and for most files it does. /etc/pacman.conf is one of the exceptions: pacman declares it a backup file, so when a version is already on disk it leaves yours alone and puts the packaged one next to it as /etc/pacman.conf.pacnew. That is why a profile can carry its own runtime configuration, and it is also why the leftover .pacnew file is worth opening and reading rather than deleting.

pieces.label: The airootfs overlay — the point
pieces.text: You have used the overlay for what it is good at — putting your own files on the image — and you have learned its two sharp edges. Permissions do not come with the copy; they come from file_permissions in profiledef.sh. And the packages are installed after your files, so a file they own is theirs unless it is a backup file.

pieces.label: Boot loaders and boot modes — scenario
pieces.text: The image builds. It boots on your laptop. It does not boot on the machine in the cupboard with the old firmware, and you have no idea why. The answer is usually two words long, and they are written in `profiledef.sh`: bootmodes. This lab is about that array, and about the menus it points at.

pieces.label: Boot loaders and boot modes — the lesson
pieces.text:
A boot loader is the program that the firmware hands control to. There are two ways a PC starts up, and they are genuinely different machines: BIOS — the old firmware, booted through a small bootloader called syslinux — and UEFI — the newer firmware, booted through GRUB or systemd-boot. A profile says which of them to bake into the image with the `bootmodes` array in profiledef.sh. Two values matter here: `bios.syslinux` for BIOS machines, and `uefi.grub` for UEFI ones. Each needs its own directory of configuration: `syslinux/` and `grub/`.

The menu entries are templates. `%INSTALL_DIR%`, `%ARCH%` and `%ARCHISO_UUID%` are placeholders that mkarchiso fills in when the image is built: the install directory, the target architecture, and the volume id of the ISO — which the initramfs uses to find the medium it booted from. That is why the same configuration file works for every build: nothing in it is hard-coded, and the same is true of the syslinux side, which uses the same placeholders in the same way.

One difference worth holding on to: in syslinux the kernel parameters live on the APPEND line; in grub they live on the `linux` line. Same parameters, different spelling.

pieces.label: Boot loaders and boot modes — The two machines
pieces.text:
BIOS: the firmware that loads a bootloader from the first megabytes of the disc. Small, simple, and still what a lot of older machines do. archiso serves it with syslinux, whose configuration lives in the profile's syslinux/ directory.

UEFI: the newer firmware, which loads a bootloader from an EFI system partition. archiso serves it with grub, whose configuration lives in the profile's grub/ directory.

An image can carry both. It cannot carry one and boot on the other, which is why bootmodes is a list and not a single value.

pieces.label: Boot loaders and boot modes — Kernel parameters
pieces.text: The kernel takes instructions on its command line: which console to use, whether to use the graphics driver, and so on. In grub they go on the line that starts with `linux`. In syslinux they go on the line that starts with APPEND. The same parameter, spelled in the place each bootloader expects.

pieces.label: Boot loaders and boot modes — task: In `profiledef.sh`, the `bootmodes` array lists only `uefi.grub`. Add `bios.syslinux` so the image also boots on a BIOS/CSM machine.
pieces.text:
In `profiledef.sh`, the `bootmodes` array lists only `uefi.grub`. Add `bios.syslinux` so the image also boots on a BIOS/CSM machine.

bootmodes is an array in profiledef.sh, one quoted string per entry. There is a line break between the two entries.

It should look like: bootmodes=('bios.syslinux'
           'uefi.grub')

The firmware decides which bootloader it looks for; the profile decides which ones are present on the disc. A UEFI machine reads the EFI system partition and finds grub; a BIOS machine reads the boot sector and finds syslinux. A profile that names only one of them builds an image that silently does nothing on the other kind of machine — and "it boots on mine" is exactly how that mistake survives a release.

pieces.label: Boot loaders and boot modes — task: Look at the grub menu entry in `grub/grub.cfg`. It loads the kernel and then the initramfs — the small filesystem the kernel unpacks into before it can mount the image. The initrd line names a file that does not exist. Fix it: the initramfs in the image is called `initramfs-linux.img`.
pieces.text:
Look at the grub menu entry in `grub/grub.cfg`. It loads the kernel and then the initramfs — the small filesystem the kernel unpacks into before it can mount the image. The initrd line names a file that does not exist. Fix it: the initramfs in the image is called `initramfs-linux.img`.

The entry has two lines that load files: one starting with linux, one starting with initrd. The initrd line names initramfs.img; the file in the image is called initramfs-linux.img.

The line should read: initrd /%INSTALL_DIR%/boot/%ARCH%/initramfs-linux.img

The kernel can only mount a root filesystem by way of the initramfs, and the initramfs is only useful if grub hands it over. Boot loaders do not search: they are told a path and they load what is there. A wrong name here gives you a black screen, which is the least informative failure mode there is.

pieces.label: Boot loaders and boot modes — task: Add a second grub menu entry, for machines whose screen comes up black because the graphics driver misbehaves. Give it a title that contains the word "safe", and have it load the same kernel — using the %INSTALL_DIR% placeholder, not a path you typed in yourself.
pieces.text:
Add a second grub menu entry, for machines whose screen comes up black because the graphics driver misbehaves. Give it a title that contains the word "safe", and have it load the same kernel — using the %INSTALL_DIR% placeholder, not a path you typed in yourself.

Copy the existing entry, change its title to something like "Vesper Linux (safe graphics)", and change the kernel parameters on the linux line.

A new block like: menuentry "Vesper Linux (safe graphics)" --id 'vesper-safe' { linux /%INSTALL_DIR%/boot/%ARCH%/vmlinuz-linux … }

A second entry is a second set of kernel parameters on the same kernel. This is how a distribution offers a fallback for a machine whose video card does not work — and it is only worth having if the path is written with the placeholders, because the path is only correct for one build.

pieces.label: Boot loaders and boot modes — task: The entry whose title contains "safe" also has to carry `%ARCHISO_UUID%`. It is not a typo and it is not a placeholder for you to fill in: mkarchiso replaces it at build time with the volume id of the finished ISO, which is how the initramfs finds the medium it was booted from.
pieces.text:
The entry whose title contains "safe" also has to carry `%ARCHISO_UUID%`. It is not a typo and it is not a placeholder for you to fill in: mkarchiso replaces it at build time with the volume id of the finished ISO, which is how the initramfs finds the medium it was booted from.

Look at the linux line of the first grub entry. It ends with archisosearchuuid=%ARCHISO_UUID%. Your new entry needs the same thing.

The linux line should end with something like: archisobasedir=%INSTALL_DIR% archisosearchuuid=%ARCHISO_UUID%

The initramfs has to find the root filesystem on the disc, and the disc has a unique volume id. The bootloader does not know it, so it cannot be written into the configuration at the time you wrote the configuration — it is filled in when the image is built. That is the whole trick behind these placeholders: one file, correct for every build.

pieces.label: Boot loaders and boot modes — task: The grub menu waits 15 seconds before it boots the default entry. Change it to 5 seconds, in `grub/grub.cfg`.
pieces.text:
The grub menu waits 15 seconds before it boots the default entry. Change it to 5 seconds, in `grub/grub.cfg`.

Near the top of grub/grub.cfg, next to the default= line, there is a timeout= line.

The line should read: timeout=5

The timeout is the difference between an image that feels quick and one that feels broken. It is set per bootloader, because each has its own menu, and a profile that carries both boot loaders should keep both timeouts in step — a mismatch is a small thing that makes a distribution feel unfinished.

pieces.label: Boot loaders and boot modes — task: Now the BIOS side. `syslinux/syslinux.cfg` has no entry in it at all. Write the one that matches the grub menu: a LABEL, a LINUX line pointing at /%INSTALL_DIR%/boot/%ARCH%/vmlinuz-linux, an INITRD line pointing at /%INSTALL_DIR%/boot/%ARCH%/initramfs-linux.img, and an APPEND line carrying `archisobasedir=%INSTALL_DIR%` and `archisosearchuuid=%ARCHISO_UUID%`.
pieces.text:
Now the BIOS side. `syslinux/syslinux.cfg` has no entry in it at all. Write the one that matches the grub menu: a LABEL, a LINUX line pointing at /%INSTALL_DIR%/boot/%ARCH%/vmlinuz-linux, an INITRD line pointing at /%INSTALL_DIR%/boot/%ARCH%/initramfs-linux.img, and an APPEND line carrying `archisobasedir=%INSTALL_DIR%` and `archisosearchuuid=%ARCHISO_UUID%`.

Syslinux entries are four lines: LABEL, MENU LABEL, LINUX, INITRD, APPEND. The LINUX and INITRD paths are the same ones the grub entry uses.

Something like:
LABEL vesper
  MENU LABEL Vesper Linux (%ARCH%, BIOS)
  LINUX /%INSTALL_DIR%/boot/%ARCH%/vmlinuz-linux
  INITRD /%INSTALL_DIR%/boot/%ARCH%/initramfs-linux.img
  APPEND archisobasedir=%INSTALL_DIR% archisosearchuuid=%ARCHISO_UUID%

The two menus are the same boot in two dialects. The paths are identical, and so are the placeholders: %INSTALL_DIR%, %ARCH% and %ARCHISO_UUID% mean exactly the same thing on both sides, and mkarchiso fills all three in at build time. A profile that gets these two out of step produces an image that boots on a UEFI laptop and not on the BIOS machine beside it.

pieces.label: Boot loaders and boot modes — task: Last one, and it is the difference between the two dialects. Add the kernel parameter `nomodeset` to BOTH menus: in grub it goes on the line starting with `linux`, in syslinux it goes on the APPEND line.
pieces.text:
Last one, and it is the difference between the two dialects. Add the kernel parameter `nomodeset` to BOTH menus: in grub it goes on the line starting with `linux`, in syslinux it goes on the APPEND line.

Two different lines in two different files. Grub: the line starting with linux. Syslinux: the line starting with APPEND.

In grub/grub.cfg, the linux line ends with something like: archisosearchuuid=%ARCHISO_UUID% nomodeset. In syslinux/syslinux.cfg, the APPEND line ends with something like: archisosearchuuid=%ARCHISO_UUID% nomodeset

Kernel parameters are instructions to the kernel, and each bootloader has its own place for them: the command line in grub, the APPEND line in syslinux. They are the same instructions in two spellings, which is why a parameter that works on one machine has to be added in two places for the other one to behave the same way.

pieces.label: Boot loaders and boot modes — the point
pieces.text: You now know how a profile claims a machine. `bootmodes` says which boot loaders go on the disc, each with its own directory of configuration, and both menus are written in templates that mkarchiso fills in at build time. The BIOS and UEFI paths are the same boot in two dialects — same placeholders, different spelling for the kernel parameters.

pieces.label: Building with mkarchiso — scenario
pieces.text: A profile is a folder of intentions. It has a name, a package list, a boot menu and a pile of opinions about permissions. None of it is an operating system yet. This is the step where the folder becomes a file you can put in a virtual machine and watch boot.

pieces.label: Building with mkarchiso — the lesson
pieces.text: `mkarchiso` is the tool that turns a profile directory into an ISO image. You point it at the profile, give it a working directory and an output directory, and it does the rest: it installs your package list into a fresh root filesystem, builds an initramfs, sets up the boot loaders you asked for, compresses the root filesystem, and writes the ISO. The command looks like this: `./archiso/mkarchiso -w work -o out profile`. `-w work` is the working directory — a scratch area mkarchiso owns and fills with a root filesystem, a boot directory and the ISO tree. `-o out` is where the finished `.iso` file lands. `profile` is the directory holding your `profiledef.sh` and `packages.x86_64`. There are three build modes: `iso`, a bootable optical image and the default; `bootstrap`, a compressed tarball of a minimal system for building a system from scratch; and `netboot`, the artifacts a machine fetches over the network to boot. You choose them with `-m iso` or `-m 'bootstrap netboot'`. One more thing matters as much as any of these: the build does not run on your laptop. It runs on a runner in your own GitLab instance, cut by GitLab CI/CD, and the ISO is published as a release download in your own repository. And the pipeline builds a commit — one specific point in your history. Changes you have not committed have never been built, and never will be.

pieces.label: Building with mkarchiso — What happens to your commit
pieces.text:
The pipeline does four things, in this order.

It checks out one commit of your profile repository. Not your working tree — a commit. If you have edited files and not committed them, the build used the old version, and the image you get back is the image of the old version.

It runs `mkarchiso -w work -o out profile` on a runner, inside an Arch container.

It boots the ISO under QEMU with the serial console as the only output, and looks for a login prompt. An image that does not boot is not a release.

It uploads the ISO as a release asset, so you can download the exact file that was tested.

pieces.label: Building with mkarchiso — The three build modes
pieces.text:
`iso` — a bootable ISO 9660 image you can write to a disc or a USB stick. This is what you want, and it is the default when you do not ask for anything else.

`bootstrap` — a compressed tarball holding a minimal system, the kind of thing you unpack onto a disk to bootstrap an installation. It uses `bootstrap_packages.<arch>` instead of `packages.<arch>`.

`netboot` — the artifacts a machine fetches over the network to boot, for a machine with no local disc.

You can ask for more than one in a single run: `-m 'iso bootstrap'`. Each mode gets its own output file, and the file names say which is which.

pieces.label: Building with mkarchiso — Reading the log
pieces.text:
The log is the build talking to you. Every line mkarchiso prints starts with `[mkarchiso] INFO:` — those are the steps it is taking. The lines without that prefix come from the other tools it runs, like `pacstrap` and `mksquashfs`.

The order of the steps tells you where a failure happened. If the log stops after "Installing packages to", the problem is in your package list or your pacman configuration. If it stops after "Creating SquashFS image", the problem is in the root filesystem options. The last thing the log says before it stops is usually the step that broke.

pieces.label: Building with mkarchiso — task: Run the build and let it finish. A build has to produce an ISO file.
pieces.text:
Run the build and let it finish. A build has to produce an ISO file.

The build panel is below the task list. The build button there queues the job on a runner.

When the build finishes the log ends with the size of the image and the URL of the release download.

The build is the point of the whole course so far. Everything up to here was a description of an image; this is the file. Its name is `<iso_name>-<iso_version>-<arch>.iso`, so the name tells you which profile and which commit produced it.

pieces.label: Building with mkarchiso — task: Check the image's volume label. It should be VESPER_202611.
pieces.text:
Check the image's volume label. It should be VESPER_202611.

The label is one of the strings near the top of profiledef.sh.

Look for the line `iso_label=`. It is usually built from the name and the build date, like `VESPER_$(date ... +%Y%m)`.

The ISO 9660 volume label is the name of the filesystem on the disc. GRUB finds the medium by searching for that label, so it has to be unique and it has to be the one your profile declares. If two of your images share a label, the bootloader may find the wrong one.

pieces.label: Building with mkarchiso — task: The image has to carry the package you added to the package list: nano.
pieces.text:
The image has to carry the package you added to the package list: nano.

The package list is `packages.x86_64` in the profile — one package name per line.

A line that starts with `#` is a comment and is not installed.

This is the check that the build is really reading your profile and not a copy of somebody else's. The package list is the shortest path from what you wrote to what the machine will actually have on disk.

pieces.label: Building with mkarchiso — task: The boot test boots the ISO in a virtual machine and watches the serial console. Did it reach a login prompt?
pieces.text:
The boot test boots the ISO in a virtual machine and watches the serial console. Did it reach a login prompt?

The boot test is the last job in the pipeline, after the ISO is written and before the release is cut.

Look for the "boot test" section of the log. It ends in either PASS or FAIL.

A successful build only means the tools did not crash. Booting is a separate question, and it is the question that catches a missing initramfs hook, a kernel without the right modules, or a boot menu pointing at a directory that is not there. The pipeline runs this test before it publishes anything, so a broken image never reaches your release page.

pieces.label: Building with mkarchiso — task: The finished ISO has to be downloadable — a release in your own repository.
pieces.text:
The finished ISO has to be downloadable — a release in your own repository.

The release lives in the group `archiso-bootcamp-academy`, in your own project.

The URL ends with `/-/releases/<tag>/downloads/<filename>`.

A release download is the artifact other people can use. It is the difference between an image that exists on your runner and an image you can hand to someone, or put on a USB stick, or boot in a virtual machine on another machine entirely.

pieces.label: Building with mkarchiso — the point
pieces.text: You have an image. It was built from one commit of your profile, on a runner, not on your laptop; it carries the packages you listed, it boots to a login prompt, and it is downloadable from your own repository. From here on, every change you make has to go through the same loop: edit, commit, build, test.

pieces.label: Reading the errors — scenario
pieces.text: Your build broke. The pipeline job went red, the ISO never appeared, and there is a wall of text between you and the answer. This is the part of ISO building that looks like luck and is not: the error is there, it is specific, and it can be read.

pieces.label: Reading the errors — the lesson
pieces.text: A build error is a message with a shape. It usually names the tool that failed — `mksquashfs`, `pacman`, `mkarchiso` — and then names the thing it choked on: an option, a file, a path. Read it from the bottom up. The first line is often a symptom, something further up that looked fine until you read it again, and the last line is the cause. The log below stopped at its very first error; the others are behind it, waiting for you to fix this one and build again. Every one of them was hit for real while building a working image, and every one of them names something specific in your profile.

pieces.label: Reading the errors — The log, from the top
pieces.text:
$ ./archiso/mkarchiso -w work -o out profile

[mkarchiso] INFO: mkarchiso configuration settings

[mkarchiso] INFO:              Architecture:   x86_64

[mkarchiso] INFO:         Working directory:   /home/runner/builds/vesper/work

[mkarchiso] INFO:    Installation directory:   vesper

[mkarchiso] INFO:          Output directory:   /home/runner/builds/vesper/out

[mkarchiso] INFO:        Current build mode:   iso

[mkarchiso] INFO:               Build modes:   iso

[mkarchiso] INFO:                  Profile:   /home/runner/builds/vesper/profile

[mkarchiso] INFO: Pacman configuration file:   /home/runner/builds/vesper/profile/pacman.conf

[mkarchiso] INFO:          Image file name:   vesper-2026.11.10-x86_64.iso

[mkarchiso] INFO:         ISO volume label:   VESPER_202611

[mkarchiso] INFO: Validating options...

[mkarchiso] INFO: Done!

[mkarchiso] INFO: Copying custom pacman.conf to work directory...

[mkarchiso] INFO: Using pacman CacheDir: /var/cache/pacman/pkg

error: config file mirrorlist could not be read: No such file or directory

pieces.label: Reading the errors — How to read it
pieces.text:
The first thing in the log is a symptom: the job failed. The last line is the cause: `error: config file mirrorlist could not be read`. Everything between them is the build doing its job successfully.

So the order of the log is a map. `[mkarchiso] INFO:` lines are steps that succeeded. The log always stops at the step that did not, and the error follows it immediately. The step before the error tells you what kind of problem you are looking at.

Three things make an error readable once you have found it: the tool that failed, the thing it was given, and the thing it was supposed to be given instead. Most build errors are one of the last two being wrong.

pieces.label: Reading the errors — The four failures in this profile
pieces.text:
The compression options in `profiledef.sh` were copied from a profile that uses a different compressor. The options belong to the compressor, not to the tool, so they do not transfer.

The `Include` in `pacman.conf` is relative. pacman resolves a relative include against the directory the build was started from, not against the directory the file is in.

The mirror in `pacman.conf` was inherited from a template. It serves package files but carries no repository databases, so pacman has nothing to resolve package names against.

The `file_permissions` entry in `profiledef.sh` names a file that is not in the image, so the path cannot be resolved inside it.

pieces.label: Reading the errors — task: Fix the root filesystem compression options in profiledef.sh so they are options the compressor you chose actually understands.
pieces.text:
Fix the root filesystem compression options in profiledef.sh so they are options the compressor you chose actually understands.

The options in `airootfs_image_tool_options` are passed straight through to mksquashfs. Ask what your compressor accepts.

`mksquashfs -help-comp zstd` lists exactly one option for zstd. `-b 1M` is fine — that one is mksquashfs's own.

The compressor options are not mksquashfs options. mksquashfs hands the list to whichever compressor you named, and each compressor accepts a different set. Upstream's releng profile uses xz, so its option list is full of xz options. Copying that list into a zstd profile gives you an error that names the compressor rather than the option — which is why the fix is to look at which compressor you chose, not to memorise option lists.

pieces.label: Reading the errors — task: Read the mksquashfs error all the way to the bottom and set the option the compressor tells you it supports.
pieces.text:
Read the mksquashfs error all the way to the bottom and set the option the compressor tells you it supports.

The second half of the error message is the useful half. It names the option the compressor takes.

`airootfs_image_tool_options=('-comp' 'zstd' '-Xcompression-level' '19' '-b' '1M')`

The second half of an error is often the better half. The first half says what went wrong; the second half says what the tool wanted instead. That is the whole distance between guessing and knowing.

pieces.label: Reading the errors — task: Make the pacman configuration resolve on its own, whatever directory the build is started from.
pieces.text:
Make the pacman configuration resolve on its own, whatever directory the build is started from.

The problem is not that the file is missing. It is that pacman looked for it in the wrong place.

Either `Include = /etc/pacman.d/mirrorlist`, or no Include at all and a `Server =` line under each repository.

This is the error that punishes you for building from a different directory than last time. `mkarchiso` calls `pacman-conf` from wherever you invoked it, and a relative Include is resolved against that directory. The reference profile avoids the trap entirely by writing the servers out in full, so the profile reads the same from anywhere.

pieces.label: Reading the errors — task: Point the repository at a mirror that actually serves the repository databases.
pieces.text:
Point the repository at a mirror that actually serves the repository databases.

A mirror that serves packages is not the same as a mirror that serves the package database.

The repository needs a line like `Server = https://geo.mirror.pkgbuild.com/$repo/os/$arch`.

The `.db` files are the indexes: they are what pacman reads to answer "what versions of nano exist". A mirror that serves packages without serving the databases is a mirror that can download a file once pacman knows its name, and nothing more. The error names a database, not a package, because the database is the first thing pacman asks for.

pieces.label: Reading the errors — task: Make every path in `file_permissions` resolve inside the image.
pieces.text:
Make every path in `file_permissions` resolve inside the image.

Which of the paths in `file_permissions` is actually in the profile's airootfs directory?

The profile ships `airootfs/etc/shadow`. It does not ship `airootfs/usr/local/bin/choose-mirror`.

Files copied out of the overlay arrive as 0644 and owned by root, with no executable bit — the overlay cannot carry permissions. `file_permissions` is the only way to set them, and it is applied to the overlay before the packages are installed, so it can only see the files your profile ships. The error says "Outside of valid path" because the path could not be resolved inside the image at all.

pieces.label: Reading the errors — the point
pieces.text: You read four build errors and fixed all four. The skill is not knowing the messages — it is knowing what to look at when you meet a message you have never seen: the tool that failed, the thing it was given, and the thing it wanted instead.

pieces.label: Testing the image — scenario
pieces.text: The pipeline went green and there is an ISO sitting in your release page. It is easy to stop here, and it is exactly where a lot of people stop by mistake. An image can be built perfectly and still be useless: it might not boot, it might boot to the wrong menu, or it might boot and then be unable to install a single package.

pieces.label: Testing the image — the lesson
pieces.text: A build that succeeds is not a build that works. Two things have to be true, and they are separate things. The first is that the image boots: it needs a kernel, an initramfs built by mkinitcpio, the mkinitcpio-archiso hook that teaches that initramfs how to find the medium it is booting from, and a bootloader that starts all of it. The second is that the image contains what you meant it to contain: your packages, your boot menu, your mirrors, and a working pacman keyring. The pipeline builds the image, boots it under QEMU with the serial console as the only output, and prints what it found. Read that report. It is telling you what is in the image, not what you meant to put in it. One of the findings it reports is the one that catches people: a missing pacman keyring. Nothing in the boot log says anything is wrong. The image boots, the login prompt appears, and pacman inside it cannot install a single package.

pieces.label: Testing the image — What the boot test actually does
pieces.text:
The image is booted under QEMU with the serial console as the only output, and the test looks for a login prompt. If there is no login prompt, the test fails and prints the last twenty-five lines of the console.

The serial console is only visible because the reference profile puts `console=tty0 console=ttyS0,115200` on the kernel command line. Without it, the test would see nothing at all and pass without having checked anything.

A kernel panic about mounting the root filesystem nearly always means one thing: the initramfs could not find the medium. Either mkinitcpio-archiso is not in the package list, so the initramfs has no idea what an ISO is, or the bootloader pointed it at the wrong place.

pieces.label: Testing the image — The keyring, which fails quietly
pieces.text:
pacman will not install anything it cannot verify. The keys it verifies against live in `/etc/pacman.d/gnupg`, and they have to be created at boot by `pacman-key --init` and `pacman-key --populate`. Neither happens on its own.

Those two commands run from `pacman-init.service`. That service declares `Requires=etc-pacman.d-gnupg.mount` — the unit that mounts a tmpfs over `/etc/pacman.d/gnupg` so the keys live in memory and not on a read-only medium.

Here is the trap: systemd treats a missing requirement as a failed dependency and drops the service. It does not print an error. The boot log says nothing at all. The image boots, the login prompt appears, and pacman cannot install anything. The test therefore does not only look for a login prompt; it also looks for the keyring mount in the log, and warns when it is not there.

Ship both units. One without the other is worse than neither, because it looks like you did the right thing.

pieces.label: Testing the image — Two pacman configurations
pieces.text:
The pacman configuration in your profile is the one the build uses. The pacman configuration inside the image is a different file, and it decides where the running system fetches packages from.

They come apart because `mkarchiso` calls `pacstrap` with `-c`, which copies the *build machine's* mirrorlist over the image's own once the transaction is done. An image that relies on `/etc/pacman.d/mirrorlist` is quietly using the builder's mirrors, not yours.

So the image needs its own mirror list, written into the overlay: `airootfs/etc/pacman.conf`. That file survives the package transaction, because `/etc/pacman.conf` is a `Backup =` file and pacman leaves an existing one alone.

pieces.label: Testing the image — task: The image has to reach a login prompt. Read the boot test in the log and fix whatever stops it.
pieces.text:
The image has to reach a login prompt. Read the boot test in the log and fix whatever stops it.

The boot test is at the bottom of the log. The last lines of the serial console are the ones worth reading.

Compare your package list with the one in the previous lab: four packages are not optional, and one of them is missing.

Booting exercises the whole chain at once: the kernel, the initramfs, the archiso hook that finds the medium, the bootloader that starts them, and the root filesystem underneath. A failure anywhere in that chain shows up here, and nowhere earlier — the build only writes files, it never runs them.

pieces.label: Testing the image — task: The boot menu has to introduce your flavour, not the default.
pieces.text:
The boot menu has to introduce your flavour, not the default.

The menu entry is in grub/grub.cfg, not in profiledef.sh.

Look for the line that starts with `menuentry`.

The boot menu is the first thing anybody sees. It is also where the image announces which install directory it is going to boot, so a menu that says one thing and boots another is a real bug, not just untidiness.

pieces.label: Testing the image — task: The image has to carry the package you put in the list: nano.
pieces.text:
The image has to carry the package you put in the list: nano.

The package list is read one name per line.

A line that starts with `#` is a comment, not a package.

This is the check that the build read *your* list and not a copy of somebody else's. It is also the check that tells you the pipeline built the commit you think it built.

pieces.label: Testing the image — task: The image has to fetch packages from the mirror you chose, not from the machine that built it.
pieces.text:
The image has to fetch packages from the mirror you chose, not from the machine that built it.

There are two pacman configurations. The one in the profile is for the build. The one in the image is in the airootfs overlay.

`profile/airootfs/etc/pacman.conf` — give it the same `Server =` lines the build-time configuration has.

An image that silently borrows the builder's mirrors will keep working right up until the builder changes, or until somebody else builds it. Writing the servers into the overlay makes the image self-contained: it carries its own idea of where packages come from, and that idea is yours.

pieces.label: Testing the image — task: The image has to be able to install packages at runtime. That needs a working pacman keyring.
pieces.text:
The image has to be able to install packages at runtime. That needs a working pacman keyring.

Two units. One runs `pacman-key --init` and `pacman-key --populate`. The other gives them somewhere to work.

The missing one is a `.mount` unit: it mounts a tmpfs over /etc/pacman.d/gnupg.

This is the failure that costs people an afternoon. The image builds, it boots, it looks perfect, and the first `pacman -S` inside it fails. The service is dropped because its requirement is missing, and systemd drops it silently. The keyring is only ever created at boot, by the two commands in that service, and they only run if the mount is there. The boot test checks for the mount in the console log precisely because nothing else will.

pieces.label: Testing the image — task: Fix everything the report found, then rebuild until the job is green.
pieces.text:
Fix everything the report found, then rebuild until the job is green.

The report at the bottom of the log lists every finding, one per line.

Fix them all, then build again. The job only goes green when every check passes.

A test you read once and ignore is worth nothing. The point of this lab is the loop: build, read the report, fix what it found, build again. That loop is how you find the problems that do not announce themselves — like a keyring that was never created.

pieces.label: Testing the image — the point
pieces.text: You built an image, booted it, read what the test said, and fixed four things the test found — one of them the kind that never makes any noise. A build that succeeds is only the beginning; the image has to boot, carry what you meant, and be able to install things when somebody sits down in front of it.

pieces.label: Making it yours — scenario
pieces.text: Everything works. The image builds, it boots, it has a keyring. It is also called Vesper, it greets people with a banner somebody else wrote, and it carries the packages somebody else chose for you. A flavour is not a copy of a working profile — it is a set of decisions somebody made, written down, and committed. This is where you make yours.

pieces.label: Making it yours — the lesson
pieces.text: You have the pieces now. The last step is making them yours: the name, the description, the packages, the look, and the banner people see when they log in. Some of it is obvious. Some of it is not, and the not-obvious part is knowing what to change and what to leave alone. The name, the label, the publisher and the application string are yours — they are free-form strings that end up in the image's metadata and on the disc. The package list is yours, but four of its entries are not optional: without `linux`, `mkinitcpio`, `mkinitcpio-archiso` and `base` you do not have an operating system, you have a directory. The boot modes, the image type and the compression options belong to the tool; leave them alone unless you know why you are changing them. And the last step of making a flavour yours is committing it. A flavour is a git repository, and the pipeline builds a commit — so a flavour that is not committed has never been built, and nobody else can build it either.

pieces.label: Making it yours — What to change
pieces.text:
`iso_name` — the first half of the output file name. It becomes the file on your release page, so keep it lower case and without spaces.

`iso_label` — the volume label on the disc, upper case, at most 32 characters. It is what the bootloader searches for, and it is usually your name and the date.

`iso_publisher` and `iso_application` — free-form strings that go into the ISO metadata. Who publishes this, and what is it for.

`packages.<arch>` — what the image has on it, and why. A package with a comment next to it is a decision; a package without one is a guess.

`airootfs/etc/motd` — the banner printed when somebody logs in.

The `menuentry` title in `grub/grub.cfg` — the boot menu.

pieces.label: Making it yours — What to leave alone
pieces.text:
`base`, `linux`, `mkinitcpio` and `mkinitcpio-archiso` in the package list. archiso cannot produce a bootable image without them, and the failure is not obvious when it happens.

The boot modes, unless you know what you are doing: dropping `uefi.grub` means the image will not boot on a modern machine.

`airootfs_image_type` and the compressor options. They decide how the root filesystem is packed, and the defaults are good.

The `bootmodes` and the packages that match them. If you add a boot loader to `bootmodes`, its package has to be in the list too.

pieces.label: Making it yours — The last step is a commit
pieces.text:
Your flavour is a git repository, and the build pipeline checks out one commit and builds that. So the state of your repository is the state of your flavour: if your changes are not committed, they have not been built, and the next person to clone your repository gets the old version.

The terminal is right there. `git status` shows you what is uncommitted, `git add .` stages the profile, and `git commit` records it.

pieces.label: Making it yours — task: Give the image your own name. It is not Vesper any more — it is yours.
pieces.text:
Give the image your own name. It is not Vesper any more — it is yours.

The name is one line near the top of profiledef.sh.

It has to be the name of your flavour, and it has to be usable in a file name.

The name is the first thing a person sees: it is the file on the release page, the directory on the ISO, and the title of the release itself. Giving it a name that means something to you is the whole difference between a working profile and a flavour.

pieces.label: Making it yours — task: The volume label has to follow the new name.
pieces.text:
The volume label has to follow the new name.

The label is the name in upper case. The date usually follows it.

`iso_label="LUMEN_202611"` — whatever your own name is, in upper case.

The volume label is how the machine finds the medium: the bootloader searches for a filesystem with that label and boots what it finds. It has to match the name you chose, and it has to be something you can type.

pieces.label: Making it yours — task: Write the publisher and the application string for your own flavour.
pieces.text:
Write the publisher and the application string for your own flavour.

They are free-form. There is no format to follow, only a truth to state.

Look at the two lines in profiledef.sh with `iso_publisher` and `iso_application` in them.

These strings are metadata, and metadata is how a disc describes itself to software and to people. "Who made this" and "what is this for" are the two questions a stranger asks when they find your image.

pieces.label: Making it yours — task: Add a package that is yours — something your flavour needs that the reference does not have — and say in a comment why it is there.
pieces.text:
Add a package that is yours — something your flavour needs that the reference does not have — and say in a comment why it is there.

One package name per line. A `#` starts a comment, and mkarchiso ignores it.

Something like `curl  # so the image can talk to the network` on its own line, or on the line above the package.

This is where a profile becomes a set of decisions rather than a list. The comment is not decoration: it is the reason the package is there, written down for the next person — which is you, in six months, wondering why you needed it.

pieces.label: Making it yours — task: Make the banner your flavour prints at login say hello.
pieces.text:
Make the banner your flavour prints at login say hello.

The motd is `airootfs/etc/motd`. It is copied into the image as it is.

The first line of the file is the line people see.

The motd is the only text in the image that is written for people rather than for the machine. It is where you can say what the flavour is, or what to do with it, or who to ask when it breaks.

pieces.label: Making it yours — task: The boot menu has to introduce your flavour too.
pieces.text:
The boot menu has to introduce your flavour too.

Look for the `menuentry` line in grub/grub.cfg.

The text between the first pair of quotes is the title.

The boot menu is the first thing on screen and the first thing a screenshot of your image shows. It is also the one piece of your flavour that everybody sees before they have even logged in.

pieces.label: Making it yours — task: Commit your flavour. The pipeline builds a commit, so anything you have not committed has not been built.
pieces.text:
Commit your flavour. The pipeline builds a commit, so anything you have not committed has not been built.

The terminal is below the files: `git status`, `git add .`, then `git commit -m "..."`.

`git commit -m "Add my flavour"` — the message can be whatever describes the change.

This is the thing the whole course has been building towards. You did not follow a recipe: you took a profile that worked, read it, changed what you wanted, and left the rest alone. What you have now is not a copy — it is a flavour, with your name on it, your packages in it, your banner on the screen. And it is in version control, which means it can be built again and again, by you and by anyone else who clones it.

pieces.label: Making it yours — the point
pieces.text: That is yours. The name, the label, the metadata, the packages, the banner and the boot menu all say the same thing, and they say it because you decided they should. The profile still looks like the one you started from, and that is the point: the parts you did not understand are still exactly where they were.
